world-3ed909c38e.headline: Democrats win largest House majority since 1992 after flipping North Carolina seat
world-3ed909c38e.fulltext:
Democrats win largest House majority since 1992 after flipping North Carolina seat
- Published
The Democratic Party has won the largest majority in the US House of Representatives since 1992, after Democrat Chuck Hubbard unseated Republican Representative Virginia Foxx in North Carolina.
The race was called on Sunday, with Hubbard beating Foxx by 330 votes with 99% counted. It was one of the closest contests of the recent midterm elections, in which Democrats also secured the Senate.
The party has now won at least 258 House seats in the midterms compared to Republicans, who hold at least 173 seats, with four races still yet to be called.
Neither party had won as many House races since 1992, when Bill Clinton won the presidency and Democrats won a total of 258 seats.
Sunday's result came after Foxx, who has represented North Carolina's 5th Congressional District since 2005, requested a recount. This is allowed under state law when the margin of victory is under 1%.
"I think the American people are just sick of what's going on and they wanted a change. They voted for change," Hubbard told the BBC News Channel after his victory. He pledged to work alongside his fellow lawmakers to hold President Donald Trump accountable.
Earlier, he wrote on X that he had spoken to Foxx, "who graciously conceded following the results of the recount process".
Hubbard added: "I deeply appreciate her commitment to a smooth transition of the office and constituent casework. We may not always agree, but we both love North Carolina and the people of the Fifth District."
Foxx, meanwhile, said in a statement: "After running a campaign focused on my track record of commonsense solutions and conservative values, I'm humbled and grateful that so many North Carolina voters responded by supporting my candidacy, even if we came up just a few votes short."
Hubbard's win, which comes after he lost to Foxx in the 2024 midterms by nine percentage points, followed a number of Democratic victories in deeply Republican districts including South Carolina, Texas, Alaska and Iowa.
Hubbard, like many Democrats running in the midterms, focused on the rising cost of living in the US during the war with Iran - a top issue for voters.
Trump himself - as well as Vice President JD Vance - have suggested inflation caused by the war in Iran was probably to blame for the Republican losses.
Hubbard has also said he will also prioritise working families and small businesses, supporting public education and expanding access to affordable healthcare, according to his website.
The remaining House races yet to be called are in Tennessee and Minnesota, while two elections in Louisiana will go to a runoff in December. In Tennessee's fourth district, Democrat Victoria Broderick leads by fewer than 300 votes, and in Minnesota's first district, Democrat Jake Johnson is winning by fewer than 500 votes.
Democrats may use their upcoming majority in the House and control of the Senate to investigate conflicts of interest and other actions by the president and those close to him, while the Senate also has the power to confirm or block the president's cabinet and judicial nominations. They will also be able to pass legislation through Congress easily, though Trump still has to give final sign off for it to become law.
However, even with control of both chambers of Congress, they will still have limits on their power as Trump can veto legislation.

india-1abd556b34.headline: Record Rs 1.22 lakh crore foreign inflows: Is India becoming the world's 'anti-AI' trade?
india-1abd556b34.fulltext:

- Business News
- India Business News
- Record Rs 1.22 lakh crore foreign inflows: Is India becoming the world's 'anti-AI' trade?
Trending
Was the artificial intelligence (AI)-led stock rally a bubble all along? Has it burst? And, is India which suffered sharp foreign outflows over the last two years for the lack of an AI story, now becoming the new favourite? Is India the world’s ‘anti-AI’ trade?Global stock markets tell a revealing story: Since the US-mid term elections, the selloff in AI-related stocks has intensified, exacerbated by the unfolding crisis at Nvidia. Since then, Nasdaq is down 7.98%. South Korea’s Kospi and Taiwan’s TAIEX - the proxies for AI trade in Asia are down 3.74% and 9.24% respectively.In contrast, India has seen record foreign investor inflows in the month of November. Foreign portfolio investors (FPIs) have remained net buyers on every trading day this month, barring the Muhurat trading session. Their cumulative purchases reached Rs 1.22 lakh crore by November 20, according to CDSL, which marks an all-time high!Sensex has risen 10.87% in November and 3.57% since the US mid-term results.The shift in FPI flows appears to indicate a broader reallocation of investments away from AI and AI-linked stocks towards India’s diversified equity market. The buying trend is expected to persist in the near term.Analysts believe that India is increasingly becoming a natural alternative for growth-focused investors seeking to diversify their exposure, as enthusiasm on Wall Street for Asian stocks linked to artificial intelligence, particularly in South Korea and Taiwan, begins to fade.

world-969b3e367a.headline: Russian warship sinks in Benghazi after suspected Ukrainian drone attack
world-969b3e367a.fulltext:
A Russian warship docked in the Libyan port city of Benghazi was struck in the early hours of Sunday in a suspected Ukrainian sea drone attack, causing a dramatic night-time explosion and the sinking of the vessel.
The strike severely damaged the Merkury, a Russian navy corvette that had stopped to refuel and take on supplies, according to Libyan officials from the country’s eastern government.
Initial reports said several Ukrainian sea drones were launched at the ship. At least four drones were intercepted and destroyed, while two hit the warship, triggering the explosion, the officials told the Associated Press.
Satellite imagery showed the Merkury had sunk after the attack, which took place in the Mediterranean, more than 1,000 miles from south Ukraine, marking a notable geographic expansion of the now near five-year war.
Though Ukraine began the war with no navy, it has developed a sea drone capability that threatened Russian warships in the Black Sea. The Russian fleet has been forced to retreat to the eastern port of Novorossiysk because Sevastopol in occupied Crimea had become unsafe.
Hours later, a Russia-linked cargo ship said to be carrying military supplies, the Ascalon, was hit by a sea drone off the coast of Benghazi. Video showed the drone heading directly towards one end of the vessel, again causing a huge explosion.
Libyan naval forces rescued the vessel’s crew, the sources added. The health ministry said some crew members were in stable condition with minor injuries. The number of injured and their nationalities are not known.
Benghazi is controlled by the self-styled Libyan National Army, led by Gen Khalifa Haftar, which controls eastern and southern Libya and has been aligned with Russia.
There was no immediate reaction from Russian authorities, and no immediate claim of responsibility for the strike, but it comes as Ukrainian forces have stepped up their long-range attacks against Russia far beyond the frontlines.
The UN mission in Libya (Unsmil) expressed “serious concern” over the two drone attacks off Benghazi and called for “an immediate, independent and transparent investigation”, in a post on X.
The eastern-based Libyan authority said port and naval base facilities, including warehouses, were safe and that normal operations would resume once the fire was brought under control and the site secured.
It condemned the suspected attack as a violation of Libya’s sovereignty and a threat to maritime safety, saying it would take legal and diplomatic measures against anyone found responsible.
“The Libyan government will not allow Libyan ports, territory or territorial waters to be turned into an arena for settling scores or exporting international conflicts,” it said.
The specialist website Naval News earlier identified the ship attacked as the Merkury, a Russian corvette – the smallest class of warship, smaller than a frigate – and said it had almost certainly been destroyed.
HI Sutton, a naval analyst, said the attack was probably conducted by sea drones, after a photograph of one emerged apparently taken off the Libyan coast. The drone, he said, “is also likely the type used in the subsequent attack”. Similar-looking drones were involved in the subsequent attack on the Ascalon cargo ship.
If it is confirmed that Ukraine has been able to blow up or seriously damage a Russian warship in Benghazi, it would represent one of its most successful naval strikes during the almost five-year war.
But it also represents a risky extension of the fighting far beyond eastern Europe, in an incident that could affect civilians on another continent and the working of the port.
A small unit of Ukrainian special forces operatives has been based at Misrata, western Libya, and is believed to have coordinated drone attacks on Russian tankers and transport ships in the past year.
Russian ships regularly make use of the port, which has a growing military importance to the Kremlin, to supply Russian mercenary forces in Africa and as a base in the Mediterranean since the country lost its bases in Syria.
Separately, a fire onboard a Russian cargo ship that was struck by drones in the Baltic Sea continued to smoulder on Sunday, Finland’s border guard said, with emergency services from Finland, Russia and Estonia working together to put out the blaze.
The Finnish military said the strike on the Sparta II on Saturday was probably carried out by Ukraine and that the vessel later drifted into Finnish waters, where it remained at anchor. The 16 crew members were evacuated on to a nearby Russian ship. One crew member was slightly injured.
On Sunday, visible flames had been put out, with operations focusing on cooling down the containers and stabilising the vessel, Finnish authorities said.
The ship, bound for the Russian exclave of Kaliningrad, had been damaged in international waters west of Russia’s Gogland Island, Finland’s defence forces said, corroborating an account by Russian officials. Kyiv has sent waves of military drones towards the Leningrad region on Russia’s north-west coast this year, including some that strayed into the airspace of nearby Baltic countries, leading to fears that the war was spilling on to Nato territory.
The risk of further attacks in the Gulf of Finland, a narrow arm of the Baltic Sea, could not be ruled out, Ivo Värk, the Estonian navy commander, told the public broadcaster ERR on Sunday.
Finland’s military said last week it had detected a strike on a Russian warship in the same area during Ukrainian drone attacks.

climate-energy-72a8c09a36.headline: UN’s COP31 Climate Conference Fizzles Out as Global Policy Divides Deepen
climate-energy-72a8c09a36.fulltext:
ANTALYA, Turkey—By the time the United Nations COP31 climate talks ended Sunday afternoon, the conference center resembled a going-out-of-business sale at a pawnshop for broken dreams.
As cleaning crews cleared away the debris left by more than 100,000 participants, Murat Kurum, president of the Conference of the Parties and Turkey’s minister of environment, urbanization and climate change, tried to tie together disparate parts of a draft climate deal with a shiny ribbon of multilateralism.
Many countries were not buying it.
For the first time since 2009, the conference ended without consensus on a cover decision, the concluding statement that typically signals global solidarity on how to confront the worsening climate crisis. Countries did adopt several decisions, including a program to help workers and communities transition away from fossil fuels, and a plan to assess progress on climate adaptation.
The failure to agree on an overarching conference statement reflected deep divisions over whether the agreement should mention fossil fuels and carbon capture, as well as how much climate financing developed countries should provide to developing nations hit by costly climate disasters.
The European Union, as well as several Latin American countries and Pacific Island states, said they would not accept the proposed text from the conference leaders.
Cover decisions at the annual conferences usually focus on new steps or language that could reinforce international efforts to slow global warming. A central aim at this meeting was to set quantifiable but voluntary global goals for the widespread electrification of economies, and to increase funding from developed countries to help developing countries adapt to climate impacts.
In 2022, the U.N. conference in Egypt agreed to establish a loss and damage fund to help vulnerable countries pay for irreversible climate impacts. A year later in Dubai, delegates from more than 190 countries agreed, for the first time, that a “just and orderly” transition away from fossil fuels in energy systems is needed to slow global warming.
Since then, international collaboration on climate issues has declined amid increased conflict, rising oil and gas prices and economic insecurity. The talks in Turkey ran two days beyond the scheduled end without reaching broad agreement on potential next steps, an outcome that won’t kill the global effort but is widely viewed as a serious setback.
But compromise for the sake of consensus is not enough, said Kathy Jetn̄il-Kijiner, a climate envoy for the Marshall Islands Ministry of the Environment.
“We will not be forced to accept false solutions,” she said. “We will not compromise our future to benefit fossil fuel interests.” As written, she added, the Antalya Pact undermines her country’s security and threatens its future.
“People are dying, seas are rising and ecosystems are collapsing,” Jetn̄il-Kijiner said. “Are we so divorced from reality that we take backward steps, even as overshoot threatens to overtake us? To accept this deal would be a betrayal to the Marshallese people.”
It’s not the first time Pacific Island nations threatened by rising seas have objected to the outcome at one of the United Nations’ annual conferences. During the 2023 U.N. talks in Dubai, a final text was adopted even though a delegation representing 39 small island developing states objected because they were still outside the plenary meeting, trying to coordinate their position.
But in Antalya, the divide ran much deeper. The economically powerful and politically influential European Union, representing 28 member countries, also rejected the proposed agreement.
Ireland’s climate, energy and environment minister, Darragh O’Brien, said the European countries formally objected to the cover decision because it fell short of what the global climate crisis demands.
“We will not endorse a decision that does not even mention fossil fuels, the key driver of climate change, and not accept a COP that greenwashes fossil fuels,” said O’Brien, speaking on behalf of the EU during Ireland’s rotating presidency.
Egypt and Brazil, hosts of the U.N. climate talks in 2023 and 2025, also criticized the text proposed by COP31 president Kurum of Turkey and Chris Bowen of Australia, president of the conference negotiations.

Liliam Beatris Chagas de Moura, director for climate at Brazil’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs, said she was disappointed that this year’s conference did not sustain the momentum from last year’s talks in her country.
Mohammad Ayoub, a climate negotiator with the Saudi Arabian energy ministry, said the 22-member League of Arab States supported the proposed Antalya Pact. He criticized developed countries for using up most of the global carbon budget, the amount of fossil fuels that can be burned without overheating the planet, and then asking developing countries to give up the very energy sources that fueled their own growth.
Ayoub condemned some countries’ opposition to including references to carbon dioxide removal and carbon capture and storage in the pact, calling their resistance to those technologies unscientific.
Carbon capture and storage are not close to being deployed fast enough “to keep 1.5 degrees within reach,” he said, referring to the long-term goal of limiting the average global temperature increase established by the 2015 Paris climate agreement.
“We believe that climate change requires all solutions on the table, and that countries select from these solutions depending on their national circumstances.”
U.N. Secretary-General António Guterres said he was “deeply disappointed” that the talks ended without consensus on an overarching agreement.
“But this setback does not change the facts,” he said. “Fossil fuels are driving the climate crisis. We can’t put out the fire while pouring fuel on it.”

ai-5f8d980aa0.headline: AI is getting better faster than experts can reliably test whether new systems are safe, METR warns
ai-5f8d980aa0.fulltext:
AI is getting better faster than experts can reliably test whether new systems are safe, METR warns
AI models are rapidly improving at AI research tasks, and they're getting harder to measure. According to the AI research organization METR, current public data isn't enough to rule out a drastic acceleration in AI research over the next few years. That could leave humans unable "to meaningfully understand, assess, and react to catastrophic risks posed by new AI systems," the organization warns.
On clearly defined coding and computational tasks with direct feedback, the models already beat experienced human professionals most of the time, METR found, though they haven't yet outperformed large groups of top experts. For tasks that take humans longer, the task length the models can handle doubles every 3.6 months. A naive extrapolation of METR's data puts them at a 50 percent success rate on the longest, 200-hour tasks by July 2027.
The systems still struggle with open-ended questions that lack immediate feedback and require real judgment, as well as with situations that are hard to recreate for training, according to METR. The organization also warns that common, easy-to-run tests may overestimate how well the models perform in real-world use, since developers train them in very similar test environments.

india-deep-tech-76cbc73687.headline: Industry body raises alarm: 689 tenders for Chinese drones & parts floated since 2021, 84% by Army
india-deep-tech-76cbc73687.source: Defence BREAKING NEWS | Defence LATEST NEWS | Defence NEWS TODAY | Defence LIVE UPDATES | Defence TRENDING NEWS | – ThePrint
india-deep-tech-76cbc73687.fulltext:
New Delhi: As many as 689 tenders floated on the Government e-Marketplace (GeM) by the military, security forces and others over nearly six years were found to specify Chinese drones and drone components, 355 of them this year alone, the Drone Federation India (DFI) has told defence officials.
The Army alone accounted for 580 (84 percent) of the tenders over the full period and 328 (92 percent) of those put up in 2026.
The Border Security Force (BSF) follows with 12 tenders (1.7 percent) over the full period. The Armed Forces Tribunal, the Controller General of Defence Accounts and the Centre for Development of Advanced Computing (C-DAC) have issued seven each (1 percent each).
The Jammu and Kashmir Police, the Directorate of Public Relations and the Directorate General of Defence Estates have five each (0.7 percent each). The remaining 61 tenders (8.9 percent) come from 44 other organisations.
Notably, GeM tenders specifying Chinese drones or drone parts nearly doubled from 190 in 2025 to 355 in 2026 up to 19 November, according to the DFI’s findings.
The DFI’s representation, dated 20 November, to the officials is based on its findings on tenders published between 10 March 2021 and 19 November 2026. The DFI says it had received reports of Army units procuring Chinese drone components, as well as knocked-down kits made up of Chinese components.
The DFI then studied publicly available bid documents on GeM and found that bids for Army procurement specify products of Chinese-linked brands, including EMAX, RunCam, SpeedyBee, RadioMaster, T-Motor, GEPRC and HGLRC. The items include motors, flight controllers, electronic speed controller (ESC) stacks, receivers, cameras and video transmission equipment, it adds.
“These are not peripheral accessories. They govern a drone’s flight, control and data transmission,” the DFI has cautioned.
The DFI is a non-government, not-for-profit industry body representing the domestic drone and counter-drone systems industry.
ThePrint reached out to the Army by email for comment. This report will be updated as and when a response is received.
“Most of the Army’s drone-related tenders from the past year or two are for drone parts, since it has recently begun assembling its own drones,” an industry source told ThePrint.
While acknowledging the Army’s role in enabling the government’s push to indigenise drones and drone components, including through initiatives such as the AASHVAST laboratory, the DFI found that 104 of the 328 flagged Army tenders from this year were raised after the laboratory was inaugurated 14 August.
An Army cybersecurity and firmware validation facility, the AASHVAST laboratory screens drones for Chinese-origin components, concealed code and remote-access mechanisms before being cleared for use.
According to the DFI’s findings, GeM tenders specifying Chinese drones or drone parts were few in the early years: six in 2021 (from 10 March), 36 in 2022, 60 in 2023 and 42 in 2024.
The sharp rise came after that. They grew 352 percent to 190 in 2025 and a further 87 percent to 355 in 2026, up to 19 November. The Army’s tenders followed the same pattern, rising from two in 2021 to 31 in 2024, then growing 419 percent to 161 in 2025 and 104 percent to 328 in 2026.
The DFI’s submission, which also seeks a meeting with officials, says the use of Chinese drones or components raises “serious security and industry concerns”.
When a bid specifically names such components, it argues, these risks enter at the tender stage itself, and it lists three risks.
First, components that units procure for their own internal use may escape further security screening, leaving units exposed to cyber vulnerabilities in flight control, communication and data. Second, with China’s export licensing of drone motors, ESCs, autopilots and radios in force from 18 November, supplies could be disrupted when they are most needed.
Third, if the user does not buy Indian components itself, the domestic component industry will not grow, and Indian manufacturers’ investments in indigenous design and secure supply chains will be undermined.
Noting that the domestic drone components ecosystem is still in its early phase, the DFI said, “It can mature only with assured demand from Indian users, and the armed forces are its most important user.”
The DFI has suggested that the authorities issue an advisory to all military formations, units and establishments to exclude Chinese components from drones and drone parts procured for internal use, including through GeM.
It has also called for reasonable preference to be given to Indian components, particularly critical parts such as flight controllers, receivers and data links, video transmitters, global navigation satellite system modules, cameras, motors, ESCs, and batteries.
Another suggestion is that a country-of-origin declaration, along with traceability at the component level, be made mandatory in all future bids related to drones, so that security is built into the specification and not left to checks after procurement.
Offering to help identify Indian alternatives at short notice, the DFI suggested that its Bharat Drone Stack Platform could be used to find Indian sources for these components. Launched in August 2025, the Bharat Drone Stack initiative lists more than 200 Indian component makers and aims to bridge the gap between them and drone integrators.
According to the DFI, the initiative targets 90 percent indigenisation in drone components by 2030, a Rs 15,000-crore domestic component market, a 75 percent cut in imports, as well as generating more than 5,000 new jobs and roping in over 500 Indian suppliers.
(Edited by Tony Rai)

science-mind-6bfc22039f.headline: Common medications may secretly rewire your gut, with effects lasting for years
science-mind-6bfc22039f.fulltext:
Common medications may secretly rewire your gut, with effects lasting for years
- Date:
- November 22, 2026
- Source:
- Estonian Research Council
- Summary:
- Medications taken years or even long ago may leave lasting changes in your gut microbiome, according to a study of more than 2,500 people. Researchers discovered that common drugs, including antidepressants, blood pressure medications, and anxiety treatments, can leave microbial “fingerprints” long after patients stop taking them. Surprisingly, some anxiety medications had effects comparable to broad-spectrum antibiotics.
- Share:
Medications you stopped taking years ago may still be influencing the bacteria living in your gut. A large study from the University of Tartu Institute of Genomics has found that many commonly prescribed drugs leave lasting changes in the gut microbiome, even long after people stop using them.
The gut microbiome is the vast community of bacteria and other microorganisms that inhabit the digestive tract. These microbes play important roles in digestion, immune function, and overall health. While antibiotics are well known for disrupting gut bacteria, the new findings suggest that many other medications can also have effects that persist for years.
To investigate these connections, researchers examined stool samples and prescription histories from more than 2,500 participants in the Estonian Biobank's Estonian Microbiome cohort. They discovered that most of the medications studied were associated with changes in gut bacteria. Even more surprisingly, a substantial number left detectable microbial "fingerprints" years after patients had stopped taking them.
Common Medications Leave Lasting Changes in Gut Bacteria
The findings extend far beyond antibiotics. Antidepressants, beta-blockers, proton pump inhibitors, and benzodiazepines were all linked to differences in the gut microbiome.
These medications are widely used to treat everyday health conditions. Beta-blockers are commonly prescribed for high blood pressure and certain heart conditions, while proton pump inhibitors reduce stomach acid and are frequently used to treat acid reflux. Benzodiazepines are often prescribed for anxiety, and antidepressants help manage depression and other mental health conditions.
"Most microbiome studies only consider current medications, but our results show that past drug use can be just as important as it is a surprisingly strong factor in explaining individual microbiome differences," said Dr. Oliver Aasmets, lead author.
This discovery suggests that looking only at the medications someone currently takes may overlook an important part of their gut health history. Previous prescriptions could help explain why the composition of gut bacteria differs so much from one person to another.
Anxiety Medications Show Effects Comparable to Antibiotics
One of the most striking findings involved benzodiazepines, a class of medications commonly used to treat anxiety.
Researchers found that these drugs were associated with changes in the gut microbiome comparable to those seen with broad-spectrum antibiotics. These antibiotics target a wide variety of bacteria and are known to substantially alter the microbial communities living in the digestive system.
The researchers also discovered that medications within the same drug class did not necessarily produce the same effects. For example, diazepam and alprazolam are both benzodiazepines used to treat similar conditions, yet they appeared to differ in how strongly they disrupted gut bacteria.
This suggests that the effects of medication on the microbiome may depend not only on the type of drug being taken, but also on the specific medication.
Gut Bacteria Can Change When Medications Are Started or Stopped
To investigate whether medications were actually contributing to these microbial changes, researchers collected additional stool samples from a smaller group of participants.
By examining how the microbiome changed when people started or stopped certain medications, the team identified predictable shifts in gut bacteria. These findings provided additional evidence that the drugs themselves were contributing to the changes, rather than simply being associated with differences already present in patients.
Although the number of participants in this follow-up analysis was relatively small, the researchers were able to verify lasting effects associated with several drug categories. These included proton pump inhibitors, selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors, and certain antibiotics, including combinations of penicillins and macrolides.
Selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors, often called SSRIs, are a widely prescribed type of antidepressant. Macrolides are a class of antibiotics used to treat various bacterial infections.
Why Your Medication History May Matter More Than Previously Thought
The findings point to an important consideration for researchers studying the relationship between gut bacteria and disease. Differences in the microbiome may reflect not only a person's current health and medication use, but also treatments received years earlier.
If previous medications are not taken into account, scientists could mistakenly attribute certain microbial differences to a disease or another health factor when past drug exposure may have contributed.
The results also highlight how much remains to be understood about the long-term relationship between medications and the gut microbiome. Although the study identified persistent microbial changes, these findings do not establish that such changes are necessarily harmful or that they lead to specific health problems.
"This is a comprehensive systematic evaluation of long-term medication effects on the microbiome using real-world medical health records," said Professor Elin Org, corresponding author. "We hope this encourages researchers and clinicians to factor in medication history when interpreting microbiome data."

Materials provided by Estonian Research Council. Note: Content may be edited for style and length.

ai-f908da6e29.headline: South Korean minister quits after AI cheating scandal engulfs university exams
ai-f908da6e29.fulltext:
South Korea’s education minister has resigned after an AI-assisted cheating scandal that erupted in the lead-up to key university entrance exams last week.
The country has been gripped by fears of AI-assisted exam cheating since last Sunday, when the top scorer in a national tax accountancy exam confessed to using a miniature camera and smartphone to achieve a near-perfect score, just four days before the crucial university entrance exam, known as the suneung.
The cheat’s confession sent officials scrambling to roll out a slew of preventive measures for the university entrance exams, including blocking public wifi in testing areas.
The unprecedented crackdown included doubling the number of supervisors and sending emergency alerts to detect any smartphones illegally smuggled into the exam centres.
Students were also told to turn up with pencils only. Erasers were provided by the test centres, as authorities tried to reduce the chances of concealed digital devices disguised as stationery.
In addition, exam-takers were asked to avoid wearing clothes with buttons. Those who failed to comply were told they would have stickers placed over the buttons to prevent the use of hidden cameras.
The government promised a reward of at least $75,000 (£57,300) for anyone reporting cheating or misconduct, with reduced penalties for those who turned in their accomplices.
But the education minister, Choi Kyo-jin, struggled to reassure the public, and teachers’ unions criticised the government response as belated.
“The exam concluded without any major incidents … However, as the minister in charge, I do not believe I am immune from public criticism that we failed to prepare adequately in advance,” Choi wrote on X. “Now that the exam is over, I take full responsibility and hereby offer my resignation.”
The president, Lee Jae Myung, accepted his resignation, the presidential office said.
The annual, eight-hour suneung determines which university a candidate can attend and, in turn, their future prospects. It is widely seen as a ticket to prestigious universities, well-paid jobs and even better marriage prospects in the highly competitive country.
Asked during a parliamentary hearing on Monday whether he was confident that authorities could catch would-be cheaters on exam day, Choi, 72, replied: “Due to my age, I am not confident I could.” His response quickly drew a public backlash.
Choi did not appear at press conferences in the days leading up to Thursday’s exam, and a vice-minister instead announced the preventive measures.
The person who cheated in the national tax accountancy exam said in a video posted to his lawyer’s YouTube account that he had photographed the questions with a concealed microcamera, sent them to an AI system and read the answers from a smartphone. “I cheated in the tax accountant exam,” he said. “My top placing is not the result of legitimate effort.”
The scandal has rattled a country where standardised tests largely dictate social mobility and career trajectories.
South Korea goes to great lengths to ensure the smooth running of the suneung. Aircraft takeoffs and landings are rescheduled during the 25-minute English listening paper to minimise noise, while artillery fire and tank movements are suspended. The stock market opens an hour late and cars are stopped 200 metres from every centre.
In the aftermath of the cheating scandal, the government announced that smart devices would have to be turned off and handed in for the suneung, while bags left in corridors would be checked for any devices that were still on. Exam officials also inspected all candidates’ glasses and watches, as well as their collars and sleeves for concealed cameras.
The government also sent emergency alerts to every phone in the country, which sounded at full volume and could not be silenced, in the hope of catching out anyone who had not handed in their device.
Officials said 111 cases of misconduct involving electronic devices were identified during Thursday’s exam, nearly half of which were detected through the emergency alerts.
A high-school student had filed a constitutional petition challenging the government’s decision to go ahead with the exam as planned. But a court rejected the request, citing insufficient evidence of irreparable harm.
Under the tightened measures, students caught cheating can be barred from retaking the exam for 10 years and face criminal prosecution.

ai-716c53fa8f.fulltext:
A new blog post from OpenAI’s chief scientist Jakub Pachocki discusses potential limits on AI development, with a focus on a measurement called perplexity.
Slowing AI development became a particularly hot topic after a former OpenAI and Anthropic researcher said the companies were “gambling with our lives,” and even Anthropic’s IPO filing suggested that the technology could pose “catastrophic or existential risks to society.”
Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei then published a plan to “pace the frontier,” seemingly endorsed by OpenAI CEO Sam Altman and SpaceX CEO Elon Musk. Among other things, Amodei called for companies to agree to “common safety standards as well as limits on the rate of unchecked AI progress.”
But to establish a speed limit on AI development, you need to agree on how you measure speed. Pachocki’s post — described by Altman as “the most important thing OpenAI has published in a while” — suggests perplexity (not to be confused with the company of the same name) could be that measurement.
In Pachochki’s argument, benchmarks that focus on AI’s “downstream capabilities” have quickly become outdated as the technology advances. But perplexity — which “measures how well a model predicts the next token on average; lower perplexity means better predictions” — has remained “informative.”
Pachochki’s post includes a chart of how the perplexity of OpenAI’s models has fallen since GPT 3.5.
“GPT‑4, at ~0.91, was proficient at utilizing chain-of-thought reasoning productively, which motivated the subsequent targeted elicitation of this capability and the creation of modern reasoning models,” he wrote. “Now, as we have reached losses below 0.8, we have seen the emergence of transformative capabilities in fields like cybersecurity and mathematics.”
So in his view, perplexity could provide the basis for “a shared benchmark for general intelligence,” which AI companies could then use to establish “common limits.” With perplexity serving as a standard measurement for AI progress, the companies would commit not to go past a certain threshold “until our ability to understand and monitor AI behavior achieves a certain concrete milestone.”

global-economics-d414aebd03.headline: Memory Chips Enter the Era of 20-Year Contracts: The AI Supply Chain Reshuffles Around a "Super Supplier"
global-economics-d414aebd03.fulltext:
Memory Chips Enter the Era of 20-Year Contracts: The AI Supply Chain Reshuffles Around a "Super Supplier"
The spread of artificial intelligence (AI) is transforming the standing of memory chips. Big Tech companies are proposing "ultra-long-term supply contracts" that commit them to buying up to 20 years' worth of output, beyond the 10-year horizon, to secure stable volumes, while also weighing equity investments, joint ventures (JVs), and direct investment in production facilities. That is the backdrop for assessments that memory makers have risen to become the "super suppliers" of the supply chain.
In a report dated the 23rd, Meritz Securities concluded that AI industry growth has turned memory chips into strategic assets that determine which global Big Tech companies will lead future businesses. Kim Sun-woo, a researcher at the brokerage, said, "SoftBank Chairman Masayoshi Son is known to have sounded out financing of $1 trillion (approximately 1,345.3 trillion won) for an acquisition of SK Hynix, centered on U.S. financial institutions," adding, "Not only SoftBank but a range of memory buyers are contemplating various forms of cooperation, including equity investment, special corporate bonds, and joint ventures."
The competition to secure memory is intensifying because supply shortages are highly likely to become a medium- to long-term bottleneck. Companies developing cutting-edge AI models and makers of computing chips believe AI will repeatedly evolve by checking its own performance and filling in gaps. In that process, memory, alongside logic and system semiconductors, is judged to be a decisive constraint. "Recently, inflation and political and personal issues have rattled the stock market with concerns about delayed AI investment and financing, but memory's presence will only become more pronounced over the medium and long term," Kim predicted.
SoftBank's moves sit at the peak of this trend. Chairman Son is understood to have proposed various measures to SK Hynix from last year through recently to secure stable volumes and capture opportunities in the high bandwidth memory (HBM) business. Beyond simple long-term agreements (LTAs), the aim is to participate in production to secure long-term volumes and attempt commercialization. SoftBank, which owns Arm, is pursuing "Izanagi ASIC," a custom chip project specialized in AI computing design, making medium- to long-term procurement of HBM and memory urgent. There is also an underlying intention to join the memory business in connection with national projects, leveraging its friendly ties with the U.S. government.
Still, industry observers see little chance of an acquisition. The biggest obstacle is the financial burden. SK Hynix's market capitalization is about $577.7 billion (approximately 777.2 trillion won), and the $1 trillion figure appears to include an acquisition premium. SoftBank Group's cash position as of the end of September 2026 was only ¥5.3934 trillion (approximately 45.7 trillion won), a scale that would require combining global investment bank acquisition financing, co-investment from private equity and sovereign wealth funds, and large-scale bond issuance. SoftBank reportedly used its Arm stake as collateral when it made an additional $10 billion (approximately 13.5 trillion won) investment in OpenAI in October; raising acquisition funds for SK Hynix the same way would require sufficient additional borrowing capacity.
Approval from the South Korean government is another hurdle. Because SK Hynix is a core company in South Korea's semiconductor industry, a foreign acquisition would require prior government approval. The fact that the largest shareholder, SK Square, holds only a 20.67% stake is another variable. With SK Group showing no willingness to sell SK Hynix, equity investments or joint ventures are bound to be extremely sensitive matters, given the risk of infringing on decision-making authority in fab operations and of technology leaks. Still, because SK Group's stake is around 20%, the minimum threshold for action is met, and some observers say a coalition of shareholders aligned with memory buyers such as SoftBank could form at any time.
The structure of contracts is itself changing. Recently, Big Tech companies including U.S. cloud service providers (CSPs) have begun proposing ultra-long-term contracts committing to purchases of more than 10 years and up to 20 years, instead of the usual three- to five-year LTAs. Related discussions are actively under way within the industry. Memory makers are reluctant to finalize production on the basis of purchase commitments alone. The burden of sharply rising fixed costs from expanding production capacity falls squarely on producers, and the trauma of past cycle downturns lingers. From the memory makers' perspective, debt investment also substantially lowers business risk compared with equity investment, which muddies decision-making authority.
The market expects a new business structure favorable to memory makers to emerge before long, beyond simple purchase contracts. Meritz Securities predicted that despite the recent sharp drop in memory makers' share prices, earnings improvement will continue through the 2027–2028 memory cycle, and an ecosystem shift favorable to the makers will drive a resilient recovery in share prices.
This case encapsulates the changing nature of semiconductor companies in the AI era. Semiconductor companies are no longer ordinary private enterprises whose ownership is determined solely by shareholders and market judgment; they are becoming strategic assets that determine national technological competitiveness and control over supply chains. The United States invoked Section 232 of the Trade Expansion Act to determine that imports of semiconductors and manufacturing equipment threaten national security, while Japan and the Netherlands manage exports of advanced equipment through licensing. South Korea also operates a system to review the impact of overseas mergers and acquisitions of companies holding core national technologies on security and the national economy. The U.S. think tank Center for Strategic and International Studies (CSIS) has analyzed that the concentration of HBM production in Asia heightens supply chain security concerns for the United States and its allies.
Ultimately, the key question is what terms memory makers can extract between volume commitments in long-term contracts and expansion of production capacity. Unlike the past, when buyers held the upper hand, assessments suggest the market is now entering a phase in which suppliers design the contract terms.

Explosions were heard in the area around Khartoum airport and other parts of the city from at around 2 a.m. until approximately 4:30 a.m. (0000-0230 GMT). A drone strike completely destroyed a house, a witness said, while a Sudanese Army source said the drones had been launched from Ethiopia.
"The drone attack at dawn today is a continuation of Ethiopian aggression against Sudanese territory, as the drones were launched from Ethiopia's Bahir Dar airport," the source told AFP. Sudan has repeatedly accused Ethiopia of allowing attacks to be launched from its territory, a claim Addis Ababa has denied.
Another witness reported that a drone hit the home of a mosque's muezzin, the person who calls Muslims to prayer, in Jebel Aulia, around 45 km (28 miles) south of Khartoum. "People were trying to rescue family members trapped under the rubble," the witness added.

OCHA condemned the risk posed to humanitarian workers, saying it was "unacceptable" that UN personnel were being exposed to such danger. Authorities did not immediately report on casualties.
The conflict, which erupted in April 2023 between the paramilitary Rapid Support Forces (RSF) and the Sudanese Army, has killed more than 2,00,000 people, aid workers estimate, and triggered the world's largest hunger and displacement crises.
The United Nations has repeatedly criticised both sides' rampant use of drones, which killed more than 1,100 people in the first half of 2026.
“Of the hundreds of child casualties this year, two-thirds were killed or injured by drone strikes,” the UN said last week. A Sudanese Army drone strike killed 15 people, including four children, in a West Kordofan village days ago, as the Army pushed through the state, recapturing territory from the RSF.
The rival forces have for the last year wrestled for control of the resource-rich southern Kordofan region, which connects the Army-held centre and east to RSF-controlled Darfur. After the final electoral rolls from the Special Intensive Revision (SIR) were published, several people whose names had been deleted challenged their exclusion. They argued that they were left out despite having completed the entire process, including attending hearings and submitting the required documents.
More than 350 appeals have been filed across Karnataka so far. The Deputy Commissioner or District Election Officer (DEO) serves as the first appellate authority in the SIR, while the Chief Electoral Officer (CEO) is the second and final appellate authority if the first-stage response is unsatisfactory. According to the CEO’s office, all appeals received so far remain pending or have been disposed of at the first appellate stage.
Officials filed Form 6
The Hindu spoke to several people in Bengaluru who have challenged their deletion. While some said officials advised them to withdraw their appeals and apply afresh through Form 6, others said officials had themselves submitted Form 6 applications on their behalf when they approached them seeking reversal of their deletion through an appeal. A few of them said they had since received an Elector’s Photo Identity Card (EPIC) and were told that their names would figure in a supplementary list.
While Form 6 applications are accepted throughout the year as part of the ECI’s “continuous updation” process, this route could leave those excluded from the SIR rolls unable to vote in the upcoming local body elections, including the Greater Bengaluru Authority (GBA) elections. The GBA elections have been directed to be conducted using the SIR final rolls by December, before even the summary revision process begins or a supplementary list is published.
Those who have appealed argue that they are not new voters seeking fresh inclusion, but people who have been voting from the same addresses and were wrongly deleted. They also questioned why they should be asked to make a declaration through Form 6 that does not reflect their circumstances, when they had already submitted documents to address the discrepancies flagged during the SIR.
Iqbal, a resident of Sarjapura, told The Hindu that he received a notice over “no mapping.” He had mapped his father’s details, whose name is on the electoral roll in Bihar,but his name was still flagged. Mr. Iqbal said that although he had shifted his residence within the city more than five years ago, his EPIC had been updated and he had submitted the required documents. His name was deleted from the final SIR rolls after figuring in the draft list.
Several people also said that while the names of all members of their families figured in the draft rolls, some were deleted from the final list. They argued that even when appeals were disposed of, the outcomes were not uniform within families.
Sahiba, a resident of Jayanagar, said she was flagged over an anomaly indicating that the age gap between two children was less than nine months. She has twins and submitted their birth certificates to establish this. However, officials subsequently raised a discrepancy in her mother’s name across records. “I explained that it was the same person and that only the spelling had changed during translation. I submitted all my documents as well as my mother’s. But I was then questioned about why I had mapped to my mother and not my father or husband. Both my father and husband are in Saudi Arabia and were not part of the 2002 rolls. Now the officials are telling me to withdraw my appeal and file Form 6,” she said.

PM Modi, Nepal PM Balendra Shah to hold talks on Nov 23; energy, connectivity on agenda
Major outcomes to expand cooperation are likely to be announced in sectors like energy, hydropower, railways, connectivity and infrastructure, the people said.
Prime Minister Narendra Modi and his Nepalese counterpart Balendra Shah will hold talks on November 23, with a focus on strengthening bilateral cooperation in energy, hydropower, railways, connectivity and infrastructure.
Shah began his two-day visit to New Delhi on Sunday afternoon. It is his first visit to India since taking office in March.
The meeting is expected to provide political direction to a significant expansion of bilateral ties in the coming years, people familiar with the matter said.
Following their talks, the two prime ministers would virtually inaugurate several projects in Nepal, the people cited above said, adding that a number of "forward-looking" bilateral documents in diverse areas are expected to be concluded and exchanged between the two sides.
This visit comes at an opportune time, as there is considerable synergy between the national priorities of both countries regarding economic growth, social development, infrastructure expansion, technology adoption and addressing issues like natural disasters and climate change, one of the people said.
It is learnt that the two sides are also set to explore ways to enhance bilateral economic engagement.
India is Nepal's largest trade, transit and investment partner and the Himalayan nation enjoys duty-free access to the Indian market.
India is also Nepal's biggest export destination, receiving about 80 per cent of Nepal's goods exports.
India is also the largest source of foreign investment in Nepal, accounting for almost one-third of the total foreign direct investment received by the country.
Both sides have nurtured a comprehensive development partnership that is one of the key pillars of bilateral interaction, featuring numerous operational and ongoing projects and initiatives.
In 2025-26, Nepal's revenue from net electricity exports to India was approximately 1800 crore Nepalese Rupees.
India and Nepal share a substantial partnership in the field of energy, where the long-term supply agreement plays a key role in meeting the neighbouring country's energy requirements.
In the connectivity sector, both sides are discussing new possibilities such as the Raxaul-Kathmandu railway link, which could open new avenues for cross-border passenger and freight connectivity.
A new passenger train service will commence between Ayodhya and Janakpur Dham, connecting two of the most revered centres of the Ramayana tradition, the people cited above said.
Nepal is important for India in the context of its overall strategic interests in the region, and leaders of the two countries have often noted the age-old "Roti Beti" relationship.
Land-locked Nepal relies heavily on India for the transportation of goods and services.
Nepal's access to the sea is through India and it imports a predominant proportion of its requirements from and through India.
In May, the bilateral relations came under some unease following Shah's remarks seeking involvement of China and the United Kingdom to address the long-standing border dispute between India and Nepal.
Days later, New Delhi categorically rejected any role for third parties to resolve its boundary row with Nepal, saying the two countries have an established bilateral mechanism to deal with all aspects of the border issue.
Nepal and India have had an old boundary dispute over Lipulekh, Limpiyadhura and Kalapani.
India has consistently maintained that the territories are part of Uttarakhand.

New Delhi: The public sector defence shipyards that were awarded contracts to build eight Next Generation Corvettes (NGCs) for the Indian Navy have moved to outsource part of the order to the private sector, a source familiar with the matter told ThePrint on Friday, adding that an announcement could be made soon. The move will allow at least one private shipyard to build a relatively large, heavily armed frontline warship for the Indian Navy for the first time.
The Ministry of Defence (MoD) signed contracts worth Rs 53,866.50 crore for the eight corvettes on 2 November with Garden Reach Shipbuilders & Engineers Limited (GRSE), Kolkata, and Goa Shipyard Limited (GSL), Vasco da Gama, both defence public sector undertaking (DPSU) shipyards.
“Both GRSE and GSL will outsource the construction of a total of three NGCs. The aim is to rope the private sector into major naval platform manufacturing and ensure that production capacity does not constrain naval shipbuilding,” the source said.
“This will allow at least one Indian private sector shipyard, which will be considered the partner shipyard of a public sector counterpart, to build such a large and capable frontline warship for the Indian Navy for the first time,” the source added.
While declining to identify the private shipyard that will take on the role, the source said the move was in line with the dual production pipeline initiative outlined by defence officials in recent months. Under this approach, two or more production lines including existing public sector capacity are established for the same equipment or similar categories of equipment to ensure both scale and speed of production.
“The government would like to see the public and private sectors working together,” the source said. “The thinking is that, in the case of shipbuilding, a whole-of-industry approach through public-private cooperation could lead to faster execution of contracts than is possible in isolation.”
Also Read: Japan to use Indian ranges for missile tests as New Delhi-Tokyo move to boost defence ties
Following the AMCA model
A similar dual production model is already on its way to being implemented in military aviation through the initiative for the country’s first stealth combat aircraft, the Advanced Medium Combat Aircraft (AMCA).
The AMCA is being developed through an industry partnership model. The process of selecting a company or consortium that will help develop and build its prototypes is underway, with the winning bidder expected to be announced soon.
There are three contenders: the Tata Group and two consortia led by the Kalyani Group and Larsen & Toubro (L&T), respectively. Whichever bidder is selected will end state-run Hindustan Aeronautics Limited’s (HAL) monopoly over combat aircraft manufacturing by creating an additional production line in the country.
Now, it appears that an effort is underway to replicate the same in naval shipbuilding.
What are the Next Generation Corvettes?
The eight NGCs will be built to an indigenous design developed by the Indian Navy, according to the MoD’s statement issued when the contracts were signed.
Each warship will have a deadweight tonnage of 4,950 tonnes, an endurance of 14 days at sea without replenishment and a maximum speed of 26 knots. They will have a crew of 11 officers and 139 sailors.
Powered by a combined diesel and gas turbine–cross-connect propulsion arrangement, the NGCs are designed for a range of maritime missions. These include offensive ship-to-ship and ship-to-surface missile strikes, anti-missile defence, anti-submarine warfare, escort duties, maritime interdiction operations—including visit, board, search and seizure—and local naval defence.
They will be equipped with medium-range anti-ship missiles, Israeli-Indian Medium-Range Surface-to-Air Missiles (MRSAM), torpedoes, an upgraded OTO Melara 76 mm super rapid gun mount, an AK-630 close-in weapon system, and 12.7 mm stabilised remote-controlled guns integrated with an electro-optic-based fire control system.
The sensor suite will feature an electro-optical infrared search-and-track system and an Israeli-Indian Multi-Function Surveillance, Track and Guidance Radar (MFSTAR). The corvettes will also have helicopter-operating capabilities.
Responses to queries emailed to GRSE and GSL are awaited. This report will be updated when they are received.

Prime Minister Narendra Modi on Saturday accused "red flags" of driving a semiconductor factory away from the country "50 years ago", a development a historian attributed to the Congress's "restrictive industrial policies" rather than Left protests.
Modi also accused the Congress, without naming it, of failing to eradicate poverty despite Indira Gandhi's vaunted "Garibi hatao" slogan.
The Prime Minister said at IIT Kharagpur's platinum jubilee celebrations that he had taken up these challenges and paved the way for semiconductor manufacturing and poverty removal.
“When I started the semiconductor mission, many questions were raised. ‘Why is this mission needed now? This country is making those; that country is making those. Semiconductors have been in production for the past 50 years. What will we achieve by making semiconductors now?’” Modi said.
The CPM and the Congress hit back, accusing the Prime Minister of not speaking the truth.
“Friends, you will be surprised to know that 50 years ago, a company came to India. It came to make semiconductors here. But it was shown the red flag and sent back…. This was the work of the red flag,” Modi said.
“And that is why, when I spoke about the (India) Semiconductor Mission, it was then said that it was too late now. Friends, I was determined. I said, even if we were late before, will India still just sit idle? We made a start.”
Modi said multiple semiconductor facilities had been established in just four years and the country had begun exporting chips.
While Modi did not identify the foreign company, sources referred to a post last year by Union information and broadcasting minister Ashwini Vaishnaw.
It spoke of a development in 1964, rather than “50 years ago”, and blamed the Congress rather than “red flags”, identified with the Left.
“Fairchild founder Robert Noyce came to Bharat in 1964. Licence permit raj of Congress did not allow setting up a semiconductor plant. Went to Hong Kong. Then founded Intel. Rest is history,” Vaishnaw posted on X on August 15, 2025. “Intel once again tried to set up a semiconductor unit in Bharat in 2005-06. Once again it was not allowed because of the policy paralysis of UPA regime.”
Dinesh C. Sharma, a New Delhi-based historian of technology, too, said it was not exactly the Left but “the restrictive industrial policies” of the Congress-led government in the 1960s that “prevented large-scale semiconductor and electronics manufacturing in India”.

climate-energy-98f96651ee.headline: 🇮🇳 Five million homes in India have gotten solar panels since 2024
climate-energy-98f96651ee.fulltext:
- In July 2026, five million Indian households had solar panels with a capacity of 14.9 gigawatts, about half of all rooftop solar in the country.
- The pace rose from about 5,000 new systems a day in October 2025 to over 16,000 a day in July 2026.
- According to Ember, a five-kilowatt-hour battery can cut the solar power a household sends to the grid during the day by 85 to 90 percent and shift it to the evening.
Five million households in India have put solar panels on their roofs with the help of a government subsidy. In July 2026, their panels had a combined capacity of 14.9 gigawatts. That is about half of all rooftop solar in the country, according to a report from the energy think tank Ember.
The subsidy comes from the PM Surya Ghar program, which the Indian government launched in 2024. The goal is solar panels on ten million rooftops. In the ten years before the program, about 794,000 such systems were installed in India.
Subsidies of up to $880
The government pays 30,000 rupees per kilowatt for the first two kilowatts. For the third kilowatt, it pays 18,000 rupees. A household can get at most 78,000 rupees, about $880.
Ember has done the math for a household that uses 350 kilowatt-hours of electricity a month. A three-kilowatt system then costs 165,000 rupees. After the subsidy, the household pays 87,000 rupees. The solar panels pay for themselves in 3.3 years.
The government has paid out over 280 billion rupees in subsidies directly to households. Households can also borrow money for the panels at 5.75 percent interest. Nearly 2.2 million have had such loans approved.
Over 16,000 new rooftops a day
In October 2025, about 5,000 systems were installed per day. In July 2026, the figure was over 16,000 per day, more than three times as many. July 2026 was the program's biggest month so far, with 506,000 new systems, SolarQuarter reports.
Over 232,000 people have completed training through the program. 34,219 companies are registered to sell and install the systems.
Nearly two million homes without an electricity bill
According to India's Minister of New and Renewable Energy, Pralhad Joshi, 1.9 million households in the program have an electricity bill of zero.
Households can also sell electricity they do not use themselves. In fiscal year 2024-25, over 1.2 million households sold surplus electricity to the grid. Together they earned 4.2 billion rupees, an average of about 3,500 rupees per household.
Batteries can shift solar power to the evening
Ember analyst Ruchita Shah has calculated what happens if households also get batteries. Today, households send a lot of solar power to the grid during the day and buy electricity in the evening. The grid then works almost like a free battery, Ember writes.
On the Indian power exchange, electricity cost about 1.56 rupees per kilowatt-hour during sunny hours in July 2026. In the evening, the price rose to about six times as much, up to the cap of 10 rupees.
In the state of Kerala, the capacity of rooftop solar panels equals 35 percent of the highest electricity demand. That peak comes in the evening, after the sun has set.
A five-kilowatt-hour battery connected to a three-kilowatt system cuts the solar power sent to the grid during the day by 85 to 90 percent. It shifts 1,600 to 1,800 kilowatt-hours a year to the evening. With a battery, the system costs 227,000 rupees and the payback time is about nine years. With a 50 percent subsidy for the battery, it drops to 6.3 years.
Ember proposes that the government give battery subsidies to five million households, half of the program's goal. That would provide 15 to 25 gigawatt-hours of storage in homes, at a cost of about 280 billion rupees.
Gujarat and Maharashtra lead
In July 2026, India had a total solar capacity of 164.6 gigawatts. Of that, 30.7 gigawatts was on rooftops, or 19 percent. In fiscal year 2018-19, the share was about 6 percent.
Ten states have over 85 percent of the rooftop solar capacity. Gujarat has 7,518 megawatts and Maharashtra 5,976 megawatts. Together they account for nearly 45 percent of the country's rooftop solar capacity.

climate-energy-6fc904a5c1.headline: Amazon plans $7 billion clean energy investment in India
climate-energy-6fc904a5c1.fulltext:
Nov 22 – Amazon is expanding its renewable energy footprint in India with a planned $7 billion investment in clean energy projects over the next four years, as the country races to increase electricity generation from non-fossil sources.
The commitment comes as India seeks to install 500 gigawatts of clean energy capacity by 2030, a target that could require an estimated $220 billion in financing.
Amazon said the investment would support additional renewable energy generation and help reduce emissions associated with electricity consumption across its Indian operations.
The company is already investing $4 billion in renewable energy projects in India. It has also unveiled four new wind and solar developments expected to generate a combined 934 megawatts of electricity under its existing programme.
Amazon’s Chief Sustainability Officer Kara Hurst said the latest commitment would support further development of wind and solar capacity, building on partnerships and investments made over several years.
The company, however, did not disclose the projects earmarked for the new funding or provide a breakdown of how the $7 billion would be spent.
India has significantly expanded its renewable energy capacity in recent years, with non-fossil sources accounting for more than 54 per cent of installed electricity generation capacity. The country’s energy mix still relies heavily on coal and oil.
The expansion of clean energy is increasingly important as India faces rising power demand while seeking to meet its climate targets.
Amazon’s investment also reflects growing pressure on major technology companies to secure cleaner electricity for energy-intensive operations, particularly data centres, as their demand for power continues to grow.

indian-startups-0d9c2e0c15.headline: Fintech Stocks Put MDR Dreams On Hold
indian-startups-0d9c2e0c15.fulltext: It seems India's fintech investors may have counted their chickens too early. The timeline for the much-anticipated merchant discount rate (MDR) on select UPI transactions has been deferred further down the calendar. The proposed monetisation of India’s UPI ecosystem was expected to be a post-Diwali bonus for digital payment companies, with a promise of a much-needed revenue stream after years of operating in a largely zero-MDR environment. However, uncertainty around the rollout is now weighing on investor sentiment, with shares of Paytm, Pine Labs and MobiKwik enduring a sharp correction. Consequently, the optimism that once buoyed fintech stocks is fading. As of Friday (November 20), Paytm parent One 97 Communications had already fallen as much as 10.8% over the past week, while One MobiKwik Systems declined 6.6% and Pine Labs dropped 9.4% on the BSE. According to a Financial Express report, the implementation of MDR could be deferred until after the 2027 assembly elections in five states, amid concerns over potential pushback from merchants and trade associations. There has been no official confirmation of a revised implementation date. The proposed framework envisages a 0.4% MDR on eligible person-to-merchant (P2M) UPI transactions above ₹2,000, subject to a cap of ₹300 per transaction. Certain categories, including railways, telecom, insurance and fuel, are proposed to attract a flat ₹5 charge, while P2P transactions and specified small merchants would remain outside the framework. For payment companies, MDR represents more than an incremental revenue stream. It offers a route to monetise transaction volumes that have expanded rapidly but historically generated limited direct revenue. Initially scheduled for October 15, the rollout was first deferred until after Diwali. Now, the prospect of a further delay has put the earnings assumptions behind recent brokerage upgrades under scrutiny. With the market jumping the gun on UPI monetisation, what does it mean for companies like PhonePe and Razorpay that are preparing for their public-market debuts? But before answering that, let’s understand how much MDR earnings upside was priced in for Paytm, Pine Labs and MobiKwik. When The Market Jumped The MDR Gun The September MDR announcement had triggered a wave of bullish brokerage commentary on payment companies, with analysts betting that the proposed charges would improve the economics of UPI transactions and open up a new source of recurring revenue. For Paytm, the potential upside was particularly significant. Goldman Sachs estimated that the framework could generate incremental EBITDA of around ₹1,400 Cr for Paytm in FY28 under a high-end scenario. The estimate represented 43–70% of its existing FY28 EBITDA projections, highlighting the potential scale of the earnings opportunity. The brokerage maintained its buy rating on the stock. Jefferies and JM Financial raised their target price to ₹2,150. JM Financial estimated incremental revenue of ₹210 Cr in FY27 and ₹470 Cr in FY28, with incremental adjusted EBITDA reaching ₹440 Cr in FY28. Pine Labs was another expected beneficiary, given its large merchant-acquiring and payment acceptance business. Jefferies estimated an incremental revenue opportunity of ₹160 Cr by FY28, equivalent to approximately 20% of its FY28 EBIT and profit estimates, and raised its target price to ₹235 from ₹180. Emkay, meanwhile, projected ₹155 Cr in UPI MDR revenue for FY28, assuming a realised take rate of six basis points, and increased its target to ₹230 from ₹190. The opportunity was supported by Pine Labs' transaction mix. In its Q2 FY27 investor presentation, the company said more than 70% of its digital checkout point transactions were UPI-led, with monthly UPI gross transaction value (GTV) of approximately ₹20,000 Cr. More than 65% of this UPI GTV came from transactions above ₹2,000, potentially placing a significant portion of its merchant payment activity within the proposed framework. Pine Labs also said its monthly UPI GTV could reach ₹33,000–34,000 Cr by FY28. MobiKwik, too, outlined the potential benefit. During its November earnings call, cofounder Upasana Taku said MDR implementation could add at least ₹100 Cr to the company's payments revenue in FY28, although the charges would be shared among issuing banks and other payment ecosystem participants. Atul Thakkar, executive director at Anand Rathi Investment Banking, believes the recent sell-off in the fintech stocks is largely a reversal of the optimism surrounding the proposed framework. “This is MDR euphoria unwinding, not a change in the businesses,” he said. According to Thakkar, the trigger was the report of a further delay, with no new implementation date in sight. But the magnitude of the correction needs to be seen against the rally that preceded it. In the period around the September MDR announcement, Paytm rose approximately 11%, MobiKwik 12% and Pine Labs 21%. From their November highs, the stocks have fallen 8–11%, with Pine Labs returning to early-September levels. Paytm shares rose 7% to ₹1,903.05 on Thursday, hitting their highest level since listing in November 2021. “The market priced in more than a normal expectation, and that excess is what has come out,” said Thakkar of Anand Rathi. The MDR uncertainty also brings to the fore: how much of the optimism surrounding listed fintechs was fuelled by the promise of the proposed framework, and how much was grounded in the strength of their underlying businesses? Fintechs’ Other Revenue Engines All three fintech companies had reported profits in the latest quarter even without any MDR contribution. The proposed charges, therefore, were not what made their businesses viable. Instead, they offered an additional revenue stream that could improve the economics of payment processing and accelerate profitability. It is particularly relevant for Paytm. Its management has also sought to position MDR as an incremental opportunity rather than a prerequisite for growth. CFO Madhur Deora had said earlier that UPI MDR was an upside to the company's business model, not fundamental to it. The company's financial services revenue, which grew 49% YoY to ₹912 Cr in Q2 FY27, also points to the growing contribution of businesses beyond payment processing. For MobiKwik and Pine Labs, too, the case for growth extends beyond the proposed fee. MobiKwik is looking to build out its financial services business, while Pine Labs has revenue streams across affordability, issuing, online payments and international markets. The larger issue, Thakkar's assessment suggests, is not whether these companies can grow without MDR, but whether investors had begun treating the proposed framework as a more certain and immediate earnings driver than it actually was. Therefore, with the implementation date still unclear, companies may have to demonstrate that their core payment and financial services businesses can sustain growth and profitability without relying on the additional MDR contribution. MDR Overhang For Upcoming IPOs The uncertainty comes at a crucial time for India’s fintech sector, with several large private companies preparing to test the public markets. The correction in listed peers could influence valuation benchmarks of players like PhonePe. Sources told Inc42 that PhonePe is targeting an early 2027 listing (February or March) at a valuation of around $10 Bn. With approximately 45% of merchant payments, the company was expected to benefit from greater clarity on monetising its payments business. A further delay could now cloud those assumptions. Razorpay has also moved closer to its public-market debut. It is also targeting a January–March 2027 listing, with an issue size of ₹5,000-6,000 Cr and a valuation of around $5 Bn. Although Razorpay has diversified into business banking, payroll, lending and cross-border payments, payment acceptance remains central to its merchant ecosystem. Therefore, investors could scrutinise its payments margins and monetisation assumptions more closely if MDR implementation remains uncertain. All in all, the MDR delay may not derail upcoming fintech IPOs, but it could make investors more cautious. For now, companies will have to justify their valuations through profits, not just the promise of future earnings. MARKETS WATCH: NEW ISSUES, POST-IPO JOURNEY & MORE Anthropic Fervour Grips India: The Claude maker’s Nasdaq debut sparked a trading frenzy among Indian retail investors, accounting for 40% of INDmoney’s international investment activity. Its $1.5 Tn valuation also reignited questions about India’s ability to build globally competitive AI companies. UC Raises ₹2,500 Cr Through QIP: UC raised ₹2,500 Cr through a QIP, attracting bids worth over ₹15,000 Cr. The funds will fuel InstaHelp’s expansion, marketing and technology investments, even as the company’s Q2 FY27 losses more than tripled to ₹182.5 Cr. Paytm’s ₹200 Cr Singapore Bet: The fintech's board approved an investment of up to ₹200 Cr in Funding Societies’ subsidiaries, including ₹162 Cr for a 19.1% stake in CardUp. The deal includes a five-year technology partnership, strengthening Paytm’s Singapore expansion through its partner-operated model. Ribbit Capital Dumps Groww: The US-based VC firm has raised around ₹7,871 Cr from Groww’s IPO and three subsequent stake sales, selling 8.7 Cr shares at ₹219 apiece to buyers including BlackRock- and Fidelity-affiliated funds, Société Générale and Kotak Mahindra Mutual Fund.
