science-mind-84d7f2abb2.headline: Neandertal gene variant in modern human genomes tied to lower schizophrenia risk, study finds
science-mind-84d7f2abb2.fulltext:
People who carry a piece of DNA inherited from Neandertals have a slightly smaller occipital lobe, the brain area at the back of the head. The same piece goes with a lower risk of schizophrenia. Hugo Zeberg and Svante Pääbo of the Max Planck Institute for Evolutionary Anthropology in Leipzig, Germany, reported the results in PNAS on November 16, 2026.
The occipital lobe holds the visual cortex, where signals from the eyes get their first processing. Each copy of the variant goes with about 0.85 cubic centimeters less volume. Two copies mean roughly 1.7 cubic centimeters less. The scan data were adjusted for head size, so the effect points to this one lobe and not to a smaller brain overall.
The team started with four known variants tied to occipital volume. Three also occur in Africa. The fourth, a deletion of four DNA letters on chromosome 14, shows up only outside Africa. All five high-coverage Neandertal genomes carry the deletion, and both high-coverage Denisovan genomes lack it. The deletion sits on a stretch of about 59,700 letters. A block this long would not have survived since the common ancestor of Neandertals and modern humans. The odds of such an old origin come to about 1.2 in 100,000.
In brain scan data from the Oxford BIG40 resource, the deletion has the strongest tie in the whole genome to the volume of the cuneus, a visual area on the inner side of the occipital lobe. A separate study ranks the same spot second in the genome for patterns of cortical surface area. The deletion lies 24,300 letters upstream of DAAM1, a gene involved in cell organization during early brain growth. The change touches no protein code, so the effect most likely works through gene control. The region looks mostly quiet in adult brain tissue, which points to activity during development.
Carriers face lower schizophrenia risk. The odds ratio is 0.95 per copy and about 0.91 for two copies, close to 10% lower. The result holds after correction for the 16 traits tested. Bipolar disorder, depression, ADHD, autism and intelligence showed no link. Educational attainment gave a weak signal that failed correction. At most, the effect equals 13 days of schooling per copy, against an average of about 15 years.
Related article: Neanderthal genes linked to rare brain-skull disorder, study finds
The authors also asked whether Neandertal DNA as a whole lowers schizophrenia risk. Among variants in Neandertal-derived segments, 54.9% of Neandertal alleles went with lower risk, compared with 54.4% elsewhere in the genome. The gap is small and not significant, so the DAAM1 effect looks limited to this spot.
One puzzle stands. Skull casts suggest Neandertals had relatively larger occipital lobes than modern humans, yet this variant goes with a smaller lobe. The authors say many genes shape brain form, along with eye and body size, so the conflict could be only apparent. Faint links to sports clubs and religious groups in UK Biobank data failed correction, and no second group exists to check them.
The authors say the work warns against equating the size of a brain region with cognitive ability.

science-mind-9a698ba55d.headline: Alzheimer’s breakthrough exposes a hidden flaw in the brain’s cleanup system
science-mind-9a698ba55d.fulltext:
Alzheimer’s breakthrough exposes a hidden flaw in the brain’s cleanup system
- Date:
- November 21, 2026
- Source:
- University of Virginia Health System
- Summary:
- Scientists have identified a gene that helps the brain’s immune cells contain harmful plaques linked to Alzheimer’s, potentially revealing a new way to fight the disease. When the gene malfunctioned in mice, toxic buildup accelerated and cognitive abilities declined, raising hopes that restoring its function could help protect the brain.
- Share:
A gene that helps the brain contain harmful protein buildup may play a crucial role in Alzheimer's disease. Researchers at UVA Health have discovered that when this gene stops functioning properly, the brain's natural defenses become less effective, allowing toxic plaques to accumulate more rapidly. The findings could point toward new ways to detect, treat, or potentially prevent the disease.
The research, led by John Lukens, PhD, focused on a gene called CASS4, which previous studies had repeatedly linked to an increased risk of Alzheimer's. Until now, however, scientists knew little about what the gene actually does. The team discovered that CASS4 helps regulate microglia, specialized immune cells that act as the brain's cleanup and defense system. When the gene's activity was disrupted, these cells struggled to respond to harmful plaques. They also became much less effective at containing and compacting the toxic material, allowing the plaques to expand and spread more aggressively.
"These findings break new ground in our understanding of how this genetic risk factor contributes to Alzheimer's disease," said Lukens, director of UVA's Harrison Family Translational Research Center in Alzheimer's and Neurodegenerative Diseases. "Our work further suggests that defective CASS4 activity may serve as an early-onset biomarker to detect Alzheimer's and that therapeutic strategies which boost its function may offer a much-needed approach to treat this devastating brain disease."
How the Brain's Cleanup System Protects Against Alzheimer's
More than 6 million Americans are living with Alzheimer's, a progressive disease that gradually damages memory and thinking abilities. As the condition advances, people can lose the ability to recognize even their closest family members, including their own children. Alzheimer's is the sixth-leading cause of death in the United States, according to the figures cited by the researchers.
Two major changes in the brain are associated with the disease. One is the accumulation of amyloid-beta plaques, sticky deposits of protein that collect between nerve cells. The other is the formation of twisted tangles of a protein called tau. Both are hallmarks of Alzheimer's, but growing evidence suggests that the brain's immune system, particularly its microglia, also plays an important role in how the disease develops.
Microglia normally help protect the brain by responding to threats and managing harmful material. When amyloid-beta plaques appear, these immune cells can surround them with protective barriers and compress the deposits into smaller, more tightly packed structures. This containment process helps limit the damage the plaques can cause to surrounding brain tissue.
The UVA researchers found that CASS4 is important for maintaining this protective response. When the gene was disrupted in laboratory mice, microglia became less capable of controlling amyloid-beta plaques. As a result, the plaques accumulated more rapidly, nearby nerve cells called neurons suffered damage, and the animals experienced worsening cognitive function.
A Little-Known Alzheimer's Gene Reveals Its Role
"Despite CASS4 being an Alzheimer's risk gene, really nothing is known about what this gene does or how it affects the brain during disease. Our lab sought to address this major knowledge gap with this paper," said Addie Walsh, UVA physiology graduate student and first author of the paper. "These are important findings because they give us new insight into how this understudied AD risk gene functions in the brain and suggest that CASS4 may normally help microglia respond to amyloid pathology."
The researchers also discovered that losing CASS4 set off a series of changes in the activity of other genes. These widespread effects could have implications beyond Alzheimer's, potentially helping explain biological processes involved in other neurodegenerative diseases, which progressively damage nerve cells.
One of the most significant findings was where CASS4 appears to exert its influence. Scientists had previously suspected that the gene contributed to Alzheimer's primarily through its effects on neurons, the cells responsible for transmitting information throughout the brain. Instead, the new research indicates that its main role is in the immune system.
That distinction could be important for developing future treatments. Rather than focusing exclusively on neurons or the proteins that accumulate in Alzheimer's, researchers may be able to strengthen the immune cells that help protect the brain from those deposits. The UVA team believes that increasing CASS4 activity or improving microglial function could eventually offer ways to slow or prevent the disease.
A Potential New Target for Alzheimer's Treatments
"We are now actively exploring potential roles for CASS4 in multiple other neurodegenerative disorders and developing novel strategies to therapeutically target it," said Lukens, of the Department of Neuroscience at the University of Virginia School of Medicine. "Many in the field initially presumed that CASS4 was likely functioning in neurons to influence Alzheimer's. Our findings shift this paradigm by proving that CASS4 predominantly acts through the immune system. This is particularly exciting, as it has only been in recent years that immune-targeting strategies have been considered for the treatment of neurodegenerative diseases, and this remains an untapped therapeutic avenue with tremendous potential."
The findings suggest that the brain's immune defenses may offer an important opportunity for future Alzheimer's therapies. They also raise the possibility that defective CASS4 activity could eventually serve as an early warning sign of the disease, potentially helping doctors identify people at risk before more serious symptoms develop.
However, these possibilities remain to be tested. The experiments showing increased plaque buildup, neuronal damage, and cognitive decline were conducted in mice. Further research will be needed to determine whether targeting CASS4 can produce similar protective effects in humans.
The work is part of a broader effort at UVA to translate laboratory discoveries into treatments for serious diseases. Lukens leads the Harrison Family Translational Research Center in Alzheimer's and Neurodegenerative Diseases, which operates within UVA's newly established Paul and Diane Manning Institute of Biotechnology. The institute was created to accelerate the development of medicines and other therapies for complex medical conditions using advances from UVA's biomedical research programs.
Lukens is also a member of UVA's Center for Brain Immunology and Glia (BIG Center), which studies the roles of immune cells and other supporting cells in brain health and disease.
Walsh, meanwhile, is preparing to continue her research into the brain's immune system in a new position.
"I will be heading to Boston at the end of the year to start my postdoctoral research with the Neurodegeneration Team at the pharmaceutical company Novartis," she said. "I am looking forward to continuing to study microglia in neurodegeneration."
Alzheimer's Gene Discovery Published in Scientific Journal
The research was published in the Journal of Experimental Medicine. The authors are Adeline E. Walsh, Benjamin A. Davis, Joshua D. Samuels, William A. Mills III, Jessica M. Thanos, Alexis M. Johnson, Katelyn A. Moore, Michael A. Puchalski, Eric J. Steacy, Benjamin W. Wendell, Amélie Daugherty-Lopès, Adrian A. Shimpi, Ukpong B. Eyo and Lukens. The researchers reported having no financial interest in the work.
Among the contributors is Davis, a fourth-year biology student at UVA, who says participating in scientific research has helped shape his approach to problem-solving and his plans for a career in medicine.
"I think that undergraduate research develops a kind of critical thinking that is difficult to cultivate inside a classroom," he said. "My experience with research has taught me to approach questions systematically and never assume there will be a clear answer. As I prepare to apply to medical school, I know these experiences will shape how I approach clinical care and the broader field of science."

Yash Sharma, a 36-year-old Indian software engineer working at Google in San Francisco, has decided to move to the UK even though he does not have a job there. But the visa uncertainties in the US have become unbearable. After spending six years on an 
H-1B visa
, Sharma has decided to leave the US and move to the UK next month, he said to Bloomberg News. He described the US as a "golden prison", saying that the constant changes to immigration rules, limited prospects of obtaining permanent residency and fear of being unable to return after travelling abroad have taken a toll on his professional and personal life.
Sharma said he had become increasingly discouraged about his chances of converting his temporary work visa into permanent residency because of the enormous Green Card backlog facing Indian nationals. He has not travelled outside the US for 18 months because he fears he may not be allowed to return. As a result, he has missed family visits, professional conferences and trips with friends. He also explored an alternative immigration route by applying for an extraordinary ability visa, which is intended for individuals with exceptional achievements in their professional fields. But his application was rejected after months of waiting.
Sharma started exploring options outside the US and applied for the UK's Global Talent visa and received approval. The visa allows him to relocate to Britain without having secured a job beforehand and search for employment after arriving. "I've seen various administrations, and to me it's clear that there will be no actual change to the law," Sharma said.
"The US feels like a golden prison," he said.
Trump's H-1B crackdown adds to uncertainty
Trump's immigration crackdown began shortly after he returned to the White House in January 2025. While the administration initially focused on illegal immigration, its policies increasingly extended to legal immigration programmes, including the H-1B system used by American companies to recruit highly skilled foreign professionals.
In September 2025, Trump announced a $100,000 payment requirement for certain new H-1B workers seeking to enter the US from abroad.
The administration argued that the programme had been abused by employers who used lower-paid foreign workers instead of hiring American employees. The changes have created additional uncertainty for companies that depend on international talent, particularly in the technology sector.
The administration has also introduced a wage-weighted H-1B selection system, giving applicants offered higher prevailing wages better chances of being selected in the visa lottery.
For workers already in the US, the difficulties extend beyond obtaining an H-1B visa. Long waits for employment-based green cards, visa stamping delays and uncertainty over future immigration rules have made long-term planning increasingly difficult.
IBM ends visa sponsorship for most consulting jobs
American companies are also changing their approach to foreign hiring. IBM told employees this month that it would discontinue visa and green card sponsorship for the majority of positions in its IBM Consulting division. The affected employees have been given the option of continuing their work for the company from locations outside the US or leaving IBM by the end of the year.
Soon after IBM, Boston-based financial technology company Flywire announced they were also evaluating how immigration restrictions could affect its workforce and business operations.The company processes billions of dollars in payments every month for colleges and other clients. In its quarterly filing this month, Flywire said it was considering shifting hiring and product development activities to lower-cost countries where it already operates to offset rising immigration-related expenses. The company warned that difficulties in recruiting and retaining specialised employees could slow product development.
Chris Thomas, an immigration lawyer and partner at Holland & Hart in Denver, told Bloomberg that corporate clients were concerned that even an inadvertent compliance mistake could expose them to government investigations or restrictions on their ability to sponsor foreign workers.
Some companies are questioning whether navigating the increasingly complicated immigration system is worth the effort. "Some are saying it's too much, it's time to start offshoring," Thomas said. Kate Angustia, supervisory policy and practice counsel at the American Immigration Lawyers Association, warned that the uncertainty was creating instability across the immigration system. "We are creating a brain drain," she said.

SINGAPORE, Nov 23 (Reuters) - US stock futures bounced at the open on Monday, while Asian markets braced for more selling as authorities around the region readied support measures after a withering wipeout last week for tech and chip stocks at the centre of the AI boom.
Investors are questioning whether the vast sums of mostly borrowed money spent building data centres to power AI models will generate returns fast enough to repay lenders and big enough to justify some of the high stock prices.
Last week's 10% drop in the Nasdaq was its largest weekly drop since pandemic panic gripped markets in March 2020.
Nasdaq 100 futures bounced about 2% in early trade on Monday, and S&P 500 futures rose around 1%.
Japan markets are closed for a holiday on Monday but futures indicate selling pressure, while Hang Seng futures also point to a fall. Australian stocks were 0.5% lower.
The "AI trade" has for several years lifted a wide range of stocks, from switch and cable makers to electricity generators and the manufacturers of anything in the computing supply chain, but they have been under pressure in recent months from rising interest rates.
AI-related shares took a particularly sharp downturn last week as the exit of Jensen Huang, the Nvidia CEO nicknamed the "godfather of AI", and the faltering debut of AI company Anthropic, which closed 8.5% lower on its first full day of trading, pointed to a souring mood.
Taiwanese shares were down 17% for the week, their biggest weekly fall since 1990, and Friday's 10% drop for the Philadelphia semiconductor index points to more pain for Asia's chip-heavy markets, especially in Taiwan and South Korea.
Taiwan's financial regulator on Saturday ordered a further tightening of short-selling rules for stocks, while in China stock exchanges announced a batch of support measures such as easing requirements for margin financing.
South Korea will be ready to deploy market stabilisation funds immediately should the market continue to fall, the finance ministry said on Sunday, after the benchmark index last week slumped to 10-month lows.

WASHINGTON - House Democrats have secured their best general election result in decades, winning at least 258 seats in an election sweep unseen since 1992 that creates not only vast opportunities to govern but also intense pressure to deliver on campaign promises and priorities.
Democrats have gained 44 House seats so far, four more than the 40 they picked up in President Donald Trump's first midterm in 2018.
The 258-seat tally was reached Sunday after Democrat Chuck Hubbard defeated Republican Rep. Virginia Foxx in North Carolina. Four other House races remain outstanding: one each in Minnesota and Tennessee and two in Louisiana that are heading to a December runoff.
Republicans will have at least 173 seats in the minority.
The milestone in the 435-member House sets up divided government, with the Senate also in Democratic hands and with a Republican president in the White House. Emboldened Democrats are preparing a 100-day agenda to address high costs of living while also confronting Trump with a vast oversight agenda for the remainder of his second term in office.
The Democrats' majority will be bigger than any the party has seen in elections since Bill Clinton was first elected president in 1992 (258) or the election of Barack Obama in 2008 (257), yet not quite the high-water mark of the Franklin D. Roosevelt-era, which saw House Democratic majorities swell past 300.
It presents opportunities and challenges ahead.
"Like, hell yeah, we should feel pressure," said Democratic Rep. Jason Crow of Colorado, a former Army Ranger.
"There are people dying in this country and people losing their healthcare, losing their livelihoods, losing their farms, being terrorized from ICE," he said at the Capitol, referring to U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement. "If you don't feel a sense of urgency and pressure in this job, and a desperation to deliver for folks, then you don't belong under this Capitol dome."
Election rout creates a mandate to govern
The numbers underscore the extraordinary scale of Democratic wins, which spanned from the strongest Republican states to the Midwest and East Coast, as voters, angry over high prices and the Iran war and concerned over corruption, made clear their discontent with Trump.
Taking control of both the House and the Senate come January, the Democrats will carry with them the backing of voters and the expectations to deliver. The Senate Democrats won a 56-seat majority in the 100-member chamber, their biggest advantage in over a decade.
The Democrats, as part of their 100-day agenda, are planning swift votes to reverse the Republicans' Medicaid cuts and restore the Affordable Care Act tax credits the Republicans allowed to expire.
Democrats have vowed to marshal their subpoena powers and launch a flurry of investigations to exert the role of Congress as a check on presidential power. That includes plans to probe how Trump and his family have become wealthier since he returned to office. Democratic leader Hakeem Jeffries of New York, who is in line to become House speaker, has not ruled out trying to impeach Trump for a third time.
"This is a historic moment for our country. This is one of the largest classes we have seen," said progressive leader Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, D-N.Y., at the Capitol.
She called the big numbers "a mandate for change."
Rep. Tom Suozzi, a centrist Democrat from New York and an accountant by profession, said the House Democrats should focus 75% of their time on affordability issues and 25% on accountability.
"Everything should be tied back to the people - and how it's affecting the people," he said.
For example, he said, as the Democrats launch investigations into Trump's financial dealings, they should be connecting the dots: "How does that affect people's pocketbooks?"
The White House has issued a warning to Democrats over their planned probes into the administration, going as far as claiming that such investigations - a standard oversight function of Congress - may amount to "blatant criminality."
A new generation of leaders
After House Speaker Mike Johnson, R-La., struggled to keep the House functioning for the past two years with a narrow 218-214 Republican majority - meaning any few GOP lawmakers could derail the agenda - the Democrats will have a wide margin that provides the new leadership much more room to maneuver.
Jeffries, who is poised to make history as the first Black speaker of the House if his colleagues elect him to the job on Jan. 3, 2027, will be able to lose dozens of Democrats on any given vote and still have the 218 needed for passage, in the face of GOP opposition.
"We're not a monolith - people come to the caucus with different ideas - it's OK," said Rep. Troy Carter, D-La., who is expected to lead the Congressional Black Caucus.
Republicans saw their number of House seats fall to one of the lowest tallies in decades. They're far from the end of the Obama administration, when the House Republicans won 247 seats in the 2014 election and the rise of Newt Gingrich when they won 230 seats in 1994.
Rep. Jim Jordan of Ohio, who was elected by his colleagues to be the Republican leader in the minority, vowed to fight their way back to power.
"Over the next two years, House Republicans will fight for American families," Jordan said.
The GOP's highwater marks include the 1920 election, with 301 seats for House Republicans.

Democrats win largest House majority since 1992 with North Carolina seat
At least 258 US House seats are now under Democratic control, with four more midterm races yet to be decided.
The Democratic Party has won at least 258 seats in the United States House of Representatives, its highest total since 1992.
On Sunday, a congressional race in North Carolina was decided after a recount, giving Democrats their 258th House seat, as a handful of races in the 2026 midterm elections are still being counted.
The race for North Carolina’s 5th congressional district saw Democrat Chuck Hubbard defeat Republican incumbent Virginia Foxx, who has served 11 terms in Congress.
The win was symbolic of a larger political shift in North Carolina and elsewhere, as longtime Republican strongholds flipped to Democratic hands, sometimes for the first time in decades.
Foxx was first elected in 2004, and in recent years, she was the chair of the House Rules Committee. According to The Associated Press news agency, only 330 votes separated Hubbard and Foxx as of Sunday, when the race was called in the Democrat’s favour.
Four House races have yet to be called, meaning Democrats may still expand their already sizeable majority in the 435-member House.
The party has now picked up about 47 House seats. Currently, in the outgoing Congress, Democrats hold 214 seats.
But the House was not the only congressional chamber to flip in this year’s midterm elections.
In the 120th Congress, set to be sworn in on January 3, Democrats will also hold 56 seats in the US Senate, its largest majority in more than a decade.
Those majorities give the Democratic Party significant power over legislation, although President Donald Trump, a Republican, has already pledged to veto bills the party puts forward.
Experts say the Republican Party’s drubbing in the midterm elections was driven by voter frustration with issues like the cost of living, the US-Israel war on Iran, corruption and immigration raids.
It was also widely interpreted as a referendum on Trump’s second term, which began in 2025.
As of November, only 32 percent of Americans approved of Trump’s job performance, according to a poll by the news agency Reuters and the research firm Ipsos.
Democrats have framed their electoral victory as a unique opportunity to shape the final two years of Trump’s presidency.
Representative Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, a progressive who won her re-election bid in New York’s 14th congressional district, called the political shift a “mandate for change”.
“This is a historic moment for our country. This is one of the largest classes we have seen,” Ocasio-Cortez said at the US Capitol.
The party’s majority in the House will be larger than any since Democrat Bill Clinton was first elected president in 1992 with a 258-seat majority for his party.
It is also just above the 257 seats held by Democrats when Barack Obama was elected in 2008.

The strike at the Benghazi Naval Base in eastern Libya severely damaged the Merkury, a Russian navy corvette, and ignited a fire at the facility, two Libyan military officials said.

india-deep-tech-9de4388a4b.headline: Industry body raises alarm: 689 tenders for Chinese drones & parts floated since 2021, 84% by Army
india-deep-tech-9de4388a4b.fulltext:
New Delhi: As many as 689 tenders floated on the Government e-Marketplace (GeM) by the military, security forces and others over nearly six years were found to specify Chinese drones and drone components, 355 of them this year alone, the Drone Federation India (DFI) has told defence officials.
The Army alone accounted for 580 (84 percent) of the tenders over the full period and 328 (92 percent) of those put up in 2026.
The Border Security Force (BSF) follows with 12 tenders (1.7 percent) over the full period. The Armed Forces Tribunal, the Controller General of Defence Accounts and the Centre for Development of Advanced Computing (C-DAC) have issued seven each (1 percent each).
The Jammu and Kashmir Police, the Directorate of Public Relations and the Directorate General of Defence Estates have five each (0.7 percent each). The remaining 61 tenders (8.9 percent) come from 44 other organisations.
Notably, GeM tenders specifying Chinese drones or drone parts nearly doubled from 190 in 2025 to 355 in 2026 up to 19 November, according to the DFI’s findings.
The DFI’s representation, dated 20 November, to the officials is based on its findings on tenders published between 10 March 2021 and 19 November 2026. The DFI says it had received reports of Army units procuring Chinese drone components, as well as knocked-down kits made up of Chinese components.
The DFI then studied publicly available bid documents on GeM and found that bids for Army procurement specify products of Chinese-linked brands, including EMAX, RunCam, SpeedyBee, RadioMaster, T-Motor, GEPRC and HGLRC. The items include motors, flight controllers, electronic speed controller (ESC) stacks, receivers, cameras and video transmission equipment, it adds.
“These are not peripheral accessories. They govern a drone’s flight, control and data transmission,” the DFI has cautioned.
The DFI is a non-government, not-for-profit industry body representing the domestic drone and counter-drone systems industry.
ThePrint reached out to the Army by email for comment. This report will be updated as and when a response is received.
“Most of the Army’s drone-related tenders from the past year or two are for drone parts, since it has recently begun assembling its own drones,” an industry source told ThePrint.
While acknowledging the Army’s role in enabling the government’s push to indigenise drones and drone components, including through initiatives such as the AASHVAST laboratory, the DFI found that 104 of the 328 flagged Army tenders from this year were raised after the laboratory was inaugurated 14 August.
An Army cybersecurity and firmware validation facility, the AASHVAST laboratory screens drones for Chinese-origin components, concealed code and remote-access mechanisms before being cleared for use.
According to the DFI’s findings, GeM tenders specifying Chinese drones or drone parts were few in the early years: six in 2021 (from 10 March), 36 in 2022, 60 in 2023 and 42 in 2024.
The sharp rise came after that. They grew 352 percent to 190 in 2025 and a further 87 percent to 355 in 2026, up to 19 November. The Army’s tenders followed the same pattern, rising from two in 2021 to 31 in 2024, then growing 419 percent to 161 in 2025 and 104 percent to 328 in 2026.
The DFI’s submission, which also seeks a meeting with officials, says the use of Chinese drones or components raises “serious security and industry concerns”.
When a bid specifically names such components, it argues, these risks enter at the tender stage itself, and it lists three risks.
First, components that units procure for their own internal use may escape further security screening, leaving units exposed to cyber vulnerabilities in flight control, communication and data. Second, with China’s export licensing of drone motors, ESCs, autopilots and radios in force from 18 November, supplies could be disrupted when they are most needed.
Third, if the user does not buy Indian components itself, the domestic component industry will not grow, and Indian manufacturers’ investments in indigenous design and secure supply chains will be undermined.
Noting that the domestic drone components ecosystem is still in its early phase, the DFI said, “It can mature only with assured demand from Indian users, and the armed forces are its most important user.”
The DFI has suggested that the authorities issue an advisory to all military formations, units and establishments to exclude Chinese components from drones and drone parts procured for internal use, including through GeM.
It has also called for reasonable preference to be given to Indian components, particularly critical parts such as flight controllers, receivers and data links, video transmitters, global navigation satellite system modules, cameras, motors, ESCs, and batteries.
Another suggestion is that a country-of-origin declaration, along with traceability at the component level, be made mandatory in all future bids related to drones, so that security is built into the specification and not left to checks after procurement.
Offering to help identify Indian alternatives at short notice, the DFI suggested that its Bharat Drone Stack Platform could be used to find Indian sources for these components. Launched in August 2025, the Bharat Drone Stack initiative lists more than 200 Indian component makers and aims to bridge the gap between them and drone integrators.
According to the DFI, the initiative targets 90 percent indigenisation in drone components by 2030, a Rs 15,000-crore domestic component market, a 75 percent cut in imports, as well as generating more than 5,000 new jobs and roping in over 500 Indian suppliers.

South Korea education minister resigns over exam cheating scandal
- Published
South Korea's Education Minister Choi Kyo-jin has resigned over an exam cheating scandal that shocked the nation.
He said he took full responsibility for the confusion caused by last-minute measures aimed at stopping AI-assisted cheating during Thursday's annual college entrance exam, known as Suneung.
A week ago, the top scorer in the national tax accountancy exam admitted using a mini-camera, mobile phone and AI tools. This prompted officials to act urgently to detect hidden devices, including sending emergency alerts to every single mobile phone in the country.
The Suneung takes up to nine hours to complete, and it plays a big role in career trajectories of millions of South Koreans.
"As the minister in charge, I believe I cannot escape criticism that we failed to prepare in advance," Choi was quoted as saying on Sunday by South Korea's Yonhap's news agency.
"Now that the exam has concluded, I feel a deep sense of responsibility and am offering my resignation," the minister added.
South Korean President Lee Jae Myung - who has been calling for an overhaul of the current exam system - later accepted Choi's resignation.
The education ministry earlier said 111 candidates had been found with unauthorised smart devices during this year's Suneung, which was taken by about 500,000 students.
Concerns over academic dishonesty during the fiercely competitive exam had been brewing in recent weeks, after reports of candidates cheating with the help of AI devices.
These fears came to a boil last weekend, when Han Won-seok, the top tax accountancy exam scorer in April, admitted to cheating.
His confession came amid speculation over his unusually high score, with just one out of 160 questions wrong.
"I used a microcamera to photograph the test questions and sent them to an AI, then checked my answers on my smartphone to commit the cheating," the 34-year-old said in a video message.
This prompted the authorities to introduce urgent measures, with just days ahead of the Suneung.
This included sending nationwide emergency alerts on the exam day.
Three alerts were sent between 08:00 and 15:00 local time on Thursday, causing phones across the country to blare out in unison - even if they were on silent mode, and even if they belonged to tourists using data roaming.
The phones did not ring out if they were switched off or on airplane mode.
It was the first time that South Korea used its national disaster alert system to catch exam cheaters.
Candidates also had to cover up the buttons on their shirts and jackets to block any hidden cameras, and authorities conducted inspections of eyewear.
All this made even honest test takers paranoid.
Ahead of the Suneung, one high school senior told the Korea Times he was worried his horn-rimmed spectacles would be mistaken for smart glasses.
Another told Yonhap he usually wore glasses but made an effort to put on contact lenses for the Suneung to avoid raising suspicions.

world-f908da6e29.headline: South Korean minister quits after AI cheating scandal engulfs university exams

South Korea’s education minister has resigned after an AI-assisted cheating scandal that erupted in the lead-up to key university entrance exams last week.
The country has been gripped by fears of AI-assisted exam cheating since last Sunday, when the top scorer in a national tax accountancy exam confessed to using a miniature camera and smartphone to achieve a near-perfect score, just four days before the crucial university entrance exam, known as the suneung.
The cheat’s confession sent officials scrambling to roll out a slew of preventive measures for the university entrance exams, including blocking public wifi in testing areas.
The unprecedented crackdown included doubling the number of supervisors and sending emergency alerts to detect any smartphones illegally smuggled into the exam centres.
Students were also told to turn up with pencils only. Erasers were provided by the test centres, as authorities tried to reduce the chances of concealed digital devices disguised as stationery.
In addition, exam-takers were asked to avoid wearing clothes with buttons. Those who failed to comply were told they would have stickers placed over the buttons to prevent the use of hidden cameras.
The government promised a reward of at least $75,000 (£57,300) for anyone reporting cheating or misconduct, with reduced penalties for those who turned in their accomplices.
But the education minister, Choi Kyo-jin, struggled to reassure the public, and teachers’ unions criticised the government response as belated.
“The exam concluded without any major incidents … However, as the minister in charge, I do not believe I am immune from public criticism that we failed to prepare adequately in advance,” Choi wrote on X. “Now that the exam is over, I take full responsibility and hereby offer my resignation.”
The president, Lee Jae Myung, accepted his resignation, the presidential office said.
The annual, eight-hour suneung determines which university a candidate can attend and, in turn, their future prospects. It is widely seen as a ticket to prestigious universities, well-paid jobs and even better marriage prospects in the highly competitive country.
Asked during a parliamentary hearing on Monday whether he was confident that authorities could catch would-be cheaters on exam day, Choi, 72, replied: “Due to my age, I am not confident I could.” His response quickly drew a public backlash.
Choi did not appear at press conferences in the days leading up to Thursday’s exam, and a vice-minister instead announced the preventive measures.
The person who cheated in the national tax accountancy exam said in a video posted to his lawyer’s YouTube account that he had photographed the questions with a concealed microcamera, sent them to an AI system and read the answers from a smartphone. “I cheated in the tax accountant exam,” he said. “My top placing is not the result of legitimate effort.”
The scandal has rattled a country where standardised tests largely dictate social mobility and career trajectories.
South Korea goes to great lengths to ensure the smooth running of the suneung. Aircraft takeoffs and landings are rescheduled during the 25-minute English listening paper to minimise noise, while artillery fire and tank movements are suspended. The stock market opens an hour late and cars are stopped 200 metres from every centre.
In the aftermath of the cheating scandal, the government announced that smart devices would have to be turned off and handed in for the suneung, while bags left in corridors would be checked for any devices that were still on. Exam officials also inspected all candidates’ glasses and watches, as well as their collars and sleeves for concealed cameras.
The government also sent emergency alerts to every phone in the country, which sounded at full volume and could not be silenced, in the hope of catching out anyone who had not handed in their device.
Officials said 111 cases of misconduct involving electronic devices were identified during Thursday’s exam, nearly half of which were detected through the emergency alerts.
A high-school student had filed a constitutional petition challenging the government’s decision to go ahead with the exam as planned. But a court rejected the request, citing insufficient evidence of irreparable harm.
Under the tightened measures, students caught cheating can be barred from retaking the exam for 10 years and face criminal prosecution.

Drone attacks kill four near Sudan’s capital, damage UN building
The Rapid Support Forces are blamed as drones reportedly hit United Nations and government buildings, as well as Khartoum’s airport.
Drone attacks blamed on Sudan’s paramilitary Rapid Support Forces (RSF) have killed four people in and around the capital, Khartoum, and damaged a United Nations building, according to local reports and UN officials.
The attacks early on Sunday struck residential areas as Sudanese air defences responded to drones reportedly targeting government buildings and Khartoum’s airport.
The strikes have raised fresh concerns about the growing danger to civilians and aid workers as Sudan‘s war increasingly relies on drones.
Explosions were heard across the capital between approximately 2am (00:00 GMT) and 4:30am (02:30 GMT), according to witnesses cited by the AFP news agency, as the army attempted to intercept the drones.
Al Jazeera’s AlMigdad Alruhaid reported from the city of Omdurman, across the Nile from Khartoum, that three people were killed and nine wounded when a drone struck a home in northern Omdurman.
A child was also killed in a separate attack south of the capital.
In the village of Jebel Aulia, about 45km (28 miles) south of Khartoum, a witness told AFP that a drone hit the home of a mosque official who calls worshippers to prayer. Residents searched the wreckage for trapped relatives.
The UN’s humanitarian coordinator in Sudan, Denise Brown, said on Sunday that one of its buildings had been damaged while staff were inside.
The UN’s humanitarian office, which coordinates emergency relief, condemned the danger to its personnel in a civilian neighbourhood, calling it “unacceptable”.
A Sudanese army source told AFP on Sunday that the drones had been launched from neighbouring Ethiopia’s Bahir Dar airport. The allegation could not be independently verified.
Ethiopia has previously denied Sudanese accusations that it allows the RSF to carry out attacks from its territory.
Sudan has also lodged complaints with the UN Security Council, the body responsible for international peace and security, and the African Union, a continental organisation, over alleged drone operations originating in Ethiopia.
Soldiers executed
Separately on Sunday, Sudan’s government accused RSF fighters of executing captured soldiers in southeastern Blue Nile state, near the Ethiopian border.
The government condemned the alleged killings as violations of international humanitarian law. The accusation has not been independently verified.
Both the RSF and the Sudanese army are relying more frequently on drones to hit enemy targets. More than 1,100 were killed by drones in the first half of this year, according to the United Nations.
The UN Children’s Fund (UNICEF) has said that drone attacks account for about two-thirds of children killed or injured in Sudan from the period of January to September.
The war in Sudan between the army and the RSF began in April 2023. It has led to one of the world’s worst humanitarian crises, with 13 million people displaced and some regions facing famine.

PM Modi, Nepal's Balendra Shah to launch direct Ayodhya-Janakpur train today
Prime Minister Narendra Modi and Nepal PM Balendra Shah will virtually flag off the Saryu-Kamala Express connecting Ayodhya and Janakpur on Monday. Their talks are expected to focus on expanding cooperation in energy, hydropower, railways, connectivity and infrastructure.
Prime Minister Narendra Modi and his Nepalese counterpart Balendra Shah will virtually flag off the Saryu-Kamala Express, connecting Ayodhya in Uttar Pradesh with Janakpur in Nepal, from Delhi on Monday. Strengthening bilateral cooperation in energy, hydropower, railways, connectivity and infrastructure is also set to be the key focus of talks between the two leaders.
The launch of the direct train service will be among the major outcomes of Shah's two-day state visit to India, his first bilateral overseas visit since assuming office in March 2026. Railway Minister Ashwini Vaishnaw and Uttar Pradesh Chief Minister Yogi Adityanath will also participate in the flag-off event in Ayodhya.
AYODHYA-JANAKPUR TRAIN TO BOOST RAMAYAN CIRCUIT
The Saryu-Kamala Express will be available for regular service from November 28 and will cover the 604-km distance between Ayodhya Cantt and Janakpur Dham in approximately 19 hours. Passengers will not have to change trains during the journey.
The weekly service will depart from Ayodhya every Monday at 5.50 pm and reach Janakpur at 12.40 pm (Nepali time) on Tuesday. On its return journey, it will leave Janakpur at 1.10 pm every Saturday and arrive in Ayodhya at 8.10 am on Sunday.
The train will pass through Mankapur, Basti, Gorakhpur, Narkatiaganj, Raxaul, Sitamarhi, Shisho, Madhubani and Jaynagar.
It will operate with modern 17-coach LHB rakes, comprising eight AC coaches, seven sleeper coaches, one luggage and disabled-friendly coach, and one power car.
Ayodhya, regarded as the birthplace of Lord Ram, and Janakpur, believed to be the birthplace of Goddess Sita, are among the most significant centres associated with the Ramayana tradition. The direct rail link is expected to strengthen the Ramayan Circuit, boost religious tourism and create opportunities for trade, local businesses and employment in border regions.
ENERGY, HYDROPOWER AND CONNECTIVITY ON AGENDA
Meanwhile, energy, hydropower, railways, connectivity and infrastructure are expected to dominate discussions between Modi and Shah on Monday.
Shah arrived in New Delhi on Sunday afternoon and was received by Minister of State for Commerce and Industry Jitin Prasada. External Affairs Minister S Jaishankar also called on the visiting Nepalese Prime Minister in the evening.
"India cherishes the special friendship with Nepal. Look forward to his engagements with PM Narendra Modi tomorrow," Jaishankar said in a post on X.
The talks between the two leaders are expected to provide political direction for expanding bilateral cooperation in the coming years. Several projects in Nepal are likely to be virtually inaugurated following their discussions, while bilateral documents covering different areas of cooperation are also expected to be exchanged.
INDIA-NEPAL ENERGY PARTNERSHIP
India is Nepal's largest trade, transit and investment partner, with the Himalayan nation enjoying duty-free access to the Indian market. India receives around 80 per cent of Nepal's goods exports and accounts for nearly one-third of the foreign direct investment received by the country.
Energy cooperation is expected to be a major component of the discussions. Under a long-term power trade agreement, India has envisaged importing up to 10,000 MW of electricity from Nepal over 10 years. India currently imports around 1,200 MW of power from the neighbouring country annually.
Nepal has also been exporting electricity to Bangladesh through the Indian power grid since November 2024. Both countries are working to expand cross-border electricity transmission capacity through new high-capacity lines.
Indian companies are also involved in several hydropower projects in Nepal, including the 900 MW Arun-3 hydroelectric project, which is currently under construction.
In the railway sector, the two countries are exploring possibilities such as the proposed Raxaul-Kathmandu railway link to strengthen passenger and freight connectivity.
VISIT COMES AMID EFFORTS TO STRENGTHEN BILATERAL TIES
The visit comes amid efforts to strengthen traditionally close ties between the two neighbours, which share deep cultural, economic and people-to-people connections.
However, bilateral relations witnessed some unease in May after Shah called for the involvement of China and the United Kingdom in resolving the long-standing border dispute between India and Nepal.
New Delhi subsequently rejected any third-party role in resolving the boundary issue, maintaining that the two countries have an established bilateral mechanism to address it.
The dispute involves Lipulekh, Limpiyadhura and Kalapani, territories that India maintains are part of Uttarakhand.

work-careers-312970f9a4.headline: US feels like a golden prison: Google engineer on H-1B visa says he's moving to the UK without a job, say
work-careers-312970f9a4.fulltext:
Yash Sharma, a 36-year-old Indian software engineer working at Google in San Francisco, has decided to move to the UK even though he does not have a job there. But the visa uncertainties in the US have become unbearable. After spending six years on an 
H-1B visa
, Sharma has decided to leave the US and move to the UK next month, he said to Bloomberg News. He described the US as a "golden prison", saying that the constant changes to immigration rules, limited prospects of obtaining permanent residency and fear of being unable to return after travelling abroad have taken a toll on his professional and personal life.
Sharma said he had become increasingly discouraged about his chances of converting his temporary work visa into permanent residency because of the enormous Green Card backlog facing Indian nationals. He has not travelled outside the US for 18 months because he fears he may not be allowed to return. As a result, he has missed family visits, professional conferences and trips with friends. He also explored an alternative immigration route by applying for an extraordinary ability visa, which is intended for individuals with exceptional achievements in their professional fields. But his application was rejected after months of waiting.
Sharma started exploring options outside the US and applied for the UK's Global Talent visa and received approval. The visa allows him to relocate to Britain without having secured a job beforehand and search for employment after arriving. "I've seen various administrations, and to me it's clear that there will be no actual change to the law," Sharma said.
"The US feels like a golden prison," he said.
Trump's H-1B crackdown adds to uncertainty
Trump's immigration crackdown began shortly after he returned to the White House in January 2025. While the administration initially focused on illegal immigration, its policies increasingly extended to legal immigration programmes, including the H-1B system used by American companies to recruit highly skilled foreign professionals.
In September 2025, Trump announced a $100,000 payment requirement for certain new H-1B workers seeking to enter the US from abroad.
The administration argued that the programme had been abused by employers who used lower-paid foreign workers instead of hiring American employees. The changes have created additional uncertainty for companies that depend on international talent, particularly in the technology sector.
The administration has also introduced a wage-weighted H-1B selection system, giving applicants offered higher prevailing wages better chances of being selected in the visa lottery.
For workers already in the US, the difficulties extend beyond obtaining an H-1B visa. Long waits for employment-based green cards, visa stamping delays and uncertainty over future immigration rules have made long-term planning increasingly difficult.
IBM ends visa sponsorship for most consulting jobs
American companies are also changing their approach to foreign hiring. IBM told employees this month that it would discontinue visa and green card sponsorship for the majority of positions in its IBM Consulting division. The affected employees have been given the option of continuing their work for the company from locations outside the US or leaving IBM by the end of the year.
Soon after IBM, Boston-based financial technology company Flywire announced they were also evaluating how immigration restrictions could affect its workforce and business operations.The company processes billions of dollars in payments every month for colleges and other clients. In its quarterly filing this month, Flywire said it was considering shifting hiring and product development activities to lower-cost countries where it already operates to offset rising immigration-related expenses. The company warned that difficulties in recruiting and retaining specialised employees could slow product development.
Chris Thomas, an immigration lawyer and partner at Holland & Hart in Denver, told Bloomberg that corporate clients were concerned that even an inadvertent compliance mistake could expose them to government investigations or restrictions on their ability to sponsor foreign workers.
Some companies are questioning whether navigating the increasingly complicated immigration system is worth the effort. "Some are saying it's too much, it's time to start offshoring," Thomas said. Kate Angustia, supervisory policy and practice counsel at the American Immigration Lawyers Association, warned that the uncertainty was creating instability across the immigration system. "We are creating a brain drain," she said.
